question_text: Assess the effectiveness of the options available to organic and biodynamic grape growers to control pests and diseases.
paper_preamble: Theory Exam Paper One - Examiners' Report Joel Butler MW General comments This year's Paper 1, the second under the revised five paper structure, provided the opportunity to demonstrate genuine understanding of a wide range of viticultural subjects. Questions ranged from broad issues (Q2) to specific, focused ones (Q4). This year's overall pass rate on Paper 1 was similar to last year's, a significant improvement on 2013 and 2014, and reflected candidates' overall higher knowledge awareness. Yet it must be stressed that there were still many papers which a) failed to provide definitions where required; b) failed to answer both parts of a question; c) made inaccurate factual statements; d) answered questions too generally and with inadequate generic examples. Reciting arguments from viticulture textbooks, while perhaps correct, will not suffice. As always, an awareness of current technical trends, factual accuracy and concrete examples is crucial to passing this paper. We would like to emphasise again our belief that non-Native English speakers who are not extremely comfortable writing in English should write in their native language. In many cases it was difficult for Examiners to see an argument's logic and give the benefit of the doubt to the paper. 1.
theory_chair_report: Theory Chair Report - Neil Tully MW This year's Theory Exam yielded 26 full theory passes, representing a 28.9% pass rate (2015 = 32%) and 7 single paper resits (2015 = 4). There could have been more passes, and a particular characteristic of this year's Theory Exam, from the overall perspective, is the frequently uneven performance of many candidates. We often found three excellent papers alongside two which were well below the pass mark. Less often, but still seen, were very irregular performances within a single paper with one poorly handled question diminishing the overall quality of otherwise sound responses. A rigorous moderation process ensures that the final results are always fair but this unevenness held back some candidates who showed excellent potential. The unusually high number of single paper resits being offered this year is also a result of the uneven performances seen across the whole Theory Exam. This emphasises the importance of gaining a thorough knowledge of the whole syllabus. Where a candidate has particularly strong knowledge in a particular field, for example as a result of their "day job", it is vital to ensure equally strong knowledge and understanding in all areas covered by the syllabus. Theory Papers 2 and 3, and to a lesser extent 1, are technical papers, and present obvious challenges for a number of candidates. The Paper Chairs will report in detail on this, but an overall comment needs to be made here that an understanding of the principles of the underlying science of our subject is indispensable for a successful outcome in these papers. Equally indispensable in Theory Paper 5 is the ability to deploy critical thinking skills and convey the resulting output in writing. In fact, across all Theory papers there was a tendency for examples to be used as a substitute for critical thinking, in an attempt to answer the question, rather than as a support to the candidate's own answer. Examples are not answers in themselves. Finally I have to report that the overall standard of spelling has diminished once again this year. 4 2016 MW
commentary: Assess the effectiveness of the options available to organic and biodynamic grape growers to control pests and diseases. This question was answered by only one third of the candidates, and overall, not very successfully. Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications. Nor were there many papers that clearly understood the conceptual differences between organic and biodynamic options (containment vs. prevention). Some papers treated some means of control as uniquely organic, such as pheromone usage and raptor control, when in fact these are now standard practices under sustainable and even many conventional growing systems. In too many instances, examples did not distinguish between organic and biodynamic. While many papers successfully discussed pest and disease control treatments using copper or sulphur, and habitat for predator animals, too few dealt with control through canopy management. Far too many papers described, but did not assess the options as the paper requires. Quoting one Examiner: "This essay reads like a list of pests/diseases and measures growers use to address them." The question required the use of analytical skills to address fundamental decisions vital to grape growers with more limited resources relative to conventional growers. 2.

commentary: What practical options does a viticulturist have at his or her disposal to address long term changes in climate in an established vineyard? A paper answered by over half the candidates, generally successfully. Absolutely critical to success here was defining 'Long Term' and also noting the answer had to be about an established vineyard. Some form of temporal notation (25-50 years, 40-75 years), with ensuing logical consideration and concrete examples, was also necessary. Many papers simply mentioned various, current vineyard 5 issues (such as faster ripening, more drought and extreme weather issues like hail) without putting their discussion into the long-term perspective. Although a majority of papers did cover issues relating to heat, drought and canopy, few grasped that long term solutions might need to include style change. For example vines might need to be top grafted over to a more appropriate variety or clone. And although canopy management changes were considered important over the long term, few papers considered below ground management techniques to improve water retention. Good candidates often pointed out the long term option of the abandonment of legal restrictions on irrigation in European countries. The best papers considered not just the global warming aspects of long term climate change, but the opposite issues in some areas such as increased and more dramatic frost events, more powerful rainstorms and the pros and cons of hail netting, factoring in both practical and the regulatory aspects. 3.

commentary: Can Cabernet Sauvignon and Riesling be successful in the same location? While a good percentage of candidates attempted this question, few succeeded with a convincing response. Three key issues needed consideration: 1) A brief review of the requirements for both varieties; 2) definition of 'successful'; 3) definition of 'same location'. Candidates then had to take a position. A few papers misinterpreted the question to mean 'high quality' wines only. Examiners caution candidates not to read too much into a question. Given the defined scope of this question, good answers were expected to show appropriate detail of where, why, and when these two varieties can co-exist successfully. Too many papers indicated broad locations, such as Napa or Austria. Good papers more correctly cited 'meso-areas', for example Clare Valley, or Columbia Valley/Yakima Valley. A couple of insightful papers suggested Germany's Pfalz, (even though little cabernet is there, it is warm enough to ripen marginally), and Alto Adige Italy. Not enough papers considered such currently successful 'same locations' as Canada's Okanagan Valley, the Margaret River or Great Southern appellations, Oregon's Umpqua Valley or less well known but plausible locations such as Israel's Northern Galilee hills. Far too many answers showed genuine ignorance of the climatic requirements for these varieties. Good answers did note that high quality viticultural practices yield positive results even when the climate conditions are challenging, while poor papers failed to discuss the viticultural factors that can allow success for both varieties in the same location. Good candidates also acknowledged that both varieties adapt easily to different conditions, both have hard wood for overwintering, and are relatively easy to grow in many different soils and climates. 4.

Compare the main vine training systems used in the following wine regions:

commentary: Compare the main vine training systems used in the following wine regions: a. Mosel b. Alsace c. Marlborough d. Châteauneuf-du-Pape This question had the smallest number of responses, not perhaps surprising, considering its specificity. The question says "compare"- a mere description of each region's system(s) was not sufficient. It was important (and necessary for a Pass) to consider all four areas. Candidates 6 needed to think like a viticulturist/producer to know why certain systems are used in respective locations, and why others would or would not be effective. The best papers looked at how the respective systems fit into the local concept of terroir, and how they effectively dealt with the various issues of water availability, exposure, ideal varietal cropping levels, vine vigor manifestation, insolation and other factors. As an example, a couple of papers explained why the Mosel Arch system is used (steep slopes, near impossibility of using wired rows, better fruit insolation). Good papers also compared where the same systems (VSP in Mosel, Alsace) were practiced but for different situations or purposes. Some also considered how, for example in Alsace, both variety and terrain dictated different systems of VSP; cane vs arched cane, vs cordon, and differing strategies for leaf removal, pruning, air circulation and fungal prevention. The best candidates also recognised that in some areas, particularly Châteauneuf du Pape, different systems may be used for different varieties. Many simply put down bush vines/gobelet, forgetting that for Syrah guyot on wire is preferred. The nature of this question demanded concrete examples. Papers that provided 'textbook' examples sometimes reflected inexperience or lack of knowledge. 5.

commentary: What steps can a viticulturist take to provide and maintain proper vine nutrition? This relatively broad question was answered by the majority of candidates, with only moderate success. The temptation was to write too much; successful responses tended to focus on the most important themes. It was a question that required a firm understanding of the technical issues. A good working knowledge of vine nutrition issues needed to be underpinned by appropriate examples to demonstrate understanding. There are links between soil, physical, chemical and biological processes, and the nutritional status of the vine, which candidates were required to address. Candidates were expected to show awareness of modern technologies such as infrared, aerial photography, neutron probes etc. Candidates should also show that different approaches work, and not be biased towards organics. They should present a balanced essay and illustrate their argument with solid examples. High marks were given to those papers that illustrated the effective use of technology and best practice farming methods (cultivation, in row vegetation, composting, foliar applications etc) to achieve good vine nutrition. Too many papers failed to consider soil testing or petiole sampling, or issues such as suitable rootstocks for high pH soils, soil amendment or technology such as fertigation to ameliorate vine nutrition. The best responses for this question were awarded some of the highest marks for all of Paper 1, reflecting confident understanding and excellent knowledge of the subject. 6.

commentary: When and how can hail cause damage at various stages of vine growth? What methods are most effective for preventing or responding to such damage? Attempted by a good number of candidates and showing strong marks, this was a highly topical question, in the light of the previous spring's events in several regions. Good answers realised and responded to the four parts of the question: WHEN / HOW / PREVENTION / RESPONSE. Examples 7 had to be global in nature and needed to discuss the weather conditions that lead to hailstorms, when they happen, how that timing dictates type and severity of damage and how to prevent or respond appropriately. A long detailed discussion of the 'cause' of hail was unnecessary, but it was important to consider the basic mechanism and, more importantly, at what periods/conditions it becomes a serious issue, followed by an assessment of potential means of prevention or response to damage. Less successful papers omitted one or more aspects of the question. Some answered well the 'when and how', but little on response, and no mention of treatments such as re-pruning. The best papers detailed certain less obvious and immediate problems, such as strong spring hail stripping new buds and destroying the coming vintage, with quantitative repercussions for up to two years. To most candidates' credit there was good knowledge of what kind of damage occurs at specific times, though not always as clear an understanding of what to do as a result. There was plenty of discussion, not always accurate, about the methods and efficacy of such treatments such as cloud seeding, anti hail cannons or netting. Good papers did note the legal restrictions in some places for these treatments, also commenting that the rationale for these restrictions may be flawed, though more study is needed. 8

question_text: It is often noted that some wines are not perfectly clean, and have low levels of potentially faulty aromas, sometimes referred to as "funky". How can a winemaker best manage a desirable element of "funkiness" in his or her wine?
paper_preamble: 2016 MW Theory Exam Paper Two - Examiners' Report Meg Brodtmann MW General comments This was a disappointing year for Paper 2. The key problems were both gaps in knowledge and the ability to apply that knowledge. Examiners commented on the "same old" issues - answer the question asked, not what you think should have been asked; do not just brain-dump everything you know about a particular topic; demonstrate a knowledge of the entire wine industry, not just the premium end and lastly, but importantly, spelling! Candidates must understand that to communicate effectively about an idea, the information given has to be filtered and applied. Examples should be used to support arguments/statements rather than as statements of fact. Examples should also be global and cover all wine types where appropriate. It is understood that some of the more technical terms used in winemaking (i.e. microbial species) are difficult to spell but MW candidates have to spell correctly all wine words, technical, geographical etc. Candidates with poor handwriting should be encouraged to type their scripts - despite fewer handwritten papers, a number were still virtually illegible. 1.

commentary: It is often noted that some wines are not perfectly clean, and have low levels of potentially faulty aromas, sometimes referred to as "funky". How can a winemaker best manage a desirable element of "funkiness" in his or her wine?  Key Understanding: - The candidate needs to present a balanced view of the sometimes opposing notions on ideas concerning wine hygiene and demonstrate the difference between a fault and a desirable/complexing character intended to be part of the style. Controlled "funkiness" is a very different thing to random spoilage from poor winemaking practices. Candidates will need to put together a convincing argument as to what "funky" wines entail. This will require some explanation of what potentially faulty/funky aromas consist and secondly how one can best manage them. It is important that the candidates show breadth and depth of knowledge across all premium quality wine styles globally including sparkling and fortified wines. Candidates should not just discuss 'natural' wines. A question that required a tight definition of 'funk' and some good practical examples, plus an understanding of the key words 'manage' and 'desirable'. Unfortunately, a very low pass mark resulted because candidates failed in these areas. This was a topical question that should have offered plenty of opportunities for candidates to discuss one of the more interesting and controversial areas of winemaking. Passing answers were able to firstly define funkiness clearly (ideally as something belonging to the grey area between fault and complexity), clearly point to key characteristics within the winemaker's control that fall into these grey areas (4-EP/4-EG, both reduction and oxidation characters, extended skin contact, etc), and then outline some winemaking steps that would permit the winemaker to end up with a desirable amount/element. Disappointingly, far too many answers had weak, poor or no definitions of 'funk', instead subverting the question to a discussion of faults. While almost all candidates were able to identify the key 9 purveyors of 'funk' in wine, there were several that simply focused on one (usually Brett) or missed important ones. A number of other candidates were insufficiently armed with accurate technical knowledge. Almost without exception answers that failed did so for failing to answer the question. Many simply dropped a detailed list of the characteristics of Brett, oxidation or reduction, quite a number lacked accurate technical knowledge, while most simply pointed to steps to eliminate rather than manage a desirable element of Brett, oxidation, reduction etc. The predictable examples of Musar, Beaucastel, Grange etc continue to appear but these are now decades old - there is a whole world of modern winemaking examples to draw on that would make candidates' papers more distinctive and original. Overall, the Examiners commented that candidates are focussing on gathering a lot of examples and using them as a substitute for critical thinking. Some papers give a number of examples as facts, with little or no context, critical assessment and rarely a counter-example to drive home a point. Examples are well used when they support a persuasive argument, not act as substitute for one. 2.

commentary: Shape, size and material of a vessel used for fermentation and maturation are important factors in determining style and quality. Discuss with particular reference to Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. Key Understanding: - Candidates must demonstrate their understanding of what choices are available for winemakers of Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon of varying styles and quality. Strong answers must address the physical dynamics of why certain shapes / sizes / materials have a material effect upon end flavours. They should make it clear that these choices are sometimes highly grape variety specific. Candidates must be able to show depth and breadth of knowledge about which styles and qualities are produced from these two varieties globally and consider styles with reference to classic / non classic origins. They must discuss both fermentation and maturation. This question was generally better answered than most others. Candidates that performed well grasped the dimensions of possibility whilst maintaining a grip upon practicality. They also tended to acknowledge the fact that there are many wineries making excellent wines from vessels and materials that are not currently in vogue - so a palpable sense of practical realism helped strengthen their arguments. Recognition of the fact that different vessel materials and shapes and sizes do make significant differences to wine style was crucial and the best papers presented a spectrum of clearly stated causes and effects. Many candidates asserted their right to speak only of either Chardonnay or Cabernet Sauvignon and consequently limited their scope for gaining marks. It is sometimes said that the candidate has the right to control the content of the essay, but when the question specifies the varietal commentary required, it is not sufficient for a candidate to state in their introduction that they do not intend to address one or other of the named varieties. Examiners also commented that the responses were too frequently a dump of 'all I know about oak' without giving particular reference to Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. Candidates should not merely have discussed who does what but should have analysed the important factors that determine quality and style. Again, Examiners noted that candidates focussed too heavily on the premium end of the market. The best candidates covered the use of various vessels for both wine types and a range of styles. 10 3.

commentary: How can a wine's tannin profile be managed during vinification? Key understanding: The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process. A brief mention of harvesting grapes at optimum phenolic ripeness is fine but candidates must focus on the winemaking. Candidates must demonstrate an understanding of the tannin extraction processes, the use of aids to extract, add and / or fix tannins and the use of oak tannins. Candidates could also discuss microoxygenation. Mention could be made of white, sparkling, sweet and fortified wine but should focus on red winemaking. This question had the highest pass rate in the Paper. The less successful scripts tended to either offer 'all I know about tannin', in rather chatty style, or provided a lot of technical detail about the subject but were unable to interpret that detail into a sensible argument. With these types of questions a logical flow to the answer helps immensely. As winemaking is itself a flow from one activity to another, it makes sense that answers cover the winemaking process in a coherent way. A solid introduction alluding to the points that will be discussed is important. With winemaking, as the reach is often broad, keeping a focus is essential. Many candidates, even the better ones, tended to overlook the use of oenological tannins in winemaking. Points raised could have been in connection with stabilising the colour with tannin or improving structural elements of early-pressed wines. Candidates must not just focus on the premium end of the market - it could be argued that judicial tannin management is more important at "entry level" - pressing off skins before the end of primary fermentation is common practice. Many candidates tended to focus too much on fermentation and not give a full answer. For those that covered pressing, few really explained with any level of authority the way tannin can be managed in a press through fractions - fining pressing fractions (and free run) is an important way of managing tannin. In relation to the extraction process, candidates should have a clear understanding of the various cap management techniques, how they differ and why they are used. They should have also included some discussion of post fermentation maceration and other post fermentation operations that can manage tannin (ie microoxygenation, ageing in barrels, etc). Lastly, as a caution, be very wary of making derogatory remarks about certain winemaking methods (i.e. rotary fermenters). These comments can show a lack of understanding of the wine industry as a whole and can 'make the Examiners blood heat up!' (to quote one Examiner). 4.

commentary: Discuss the impact of malolactic fermentation, or its absence, on wine style. Key Understanding: This question is looking for the candidate to give a concise definition of what malolactic fermentation is and does, and then apply this to a number of wine styles outlining the relevant impact that MLF has on that style. It is important to give examples across styles from sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified to substantiate the argument. Candidates must demonstrate a thorough understanding of the MLF process - bacteria involved, fermentation temperature, possible risks - and discuss this in relation to the impact on wine style (acid reduction, bi-products of the MLF). 11 Perhaps because this question seemed fairly straightforward at first glance, a great many candidates chose it. Only one really gave an excellent and comprehensive answer along with a few passable ones. The rest seemed to struggle. The main cause of concern was a failure to define clearly the bacteria responsible for malolactic fermentation. Students need to update their knowledge of LAB strains. To start with, Oenococcus oeni has the greatest capacity to grow in an acidic environment and in the presence of 10% ethanol. It was previously called Leuconostoc oenos but the name was changed in the late 1990's and therefore scripts should be clear in referencing the current name. Oenococcus oeni is the most common species to conduct the MLF but other bacterial populations can be found and are generally considered to be spoilage bacteria. In addition several students seem convinced that Oenococcus oeni doesn't occur naturally - perhaps due to the fact that winemakers do add it as a cultured bacterium. With this in mind, students were likely to run into trouble later in the paper if their introduction wasn't watertight. It also required careful planning - this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers. The best looked to break it down into red wines, white wines/sparkling bases and other impacts such as microbiological. Too many candidates simply dismissed the impact of MLF on red wine as 'all red wines go through MLF'. Clearly, there were more marks to be gained in considering the impacts on white and sparkling wines but the impact of MLF on red wines as well as reds that don't go through MLF could have had a paragraph of discussion. Apart from Nouveau styles, there are a number of sweet red wines on the market now that do not undergo MLF. More importantly a number of candidates attempted the question centred almost exclusively on the impact of MLF on Chardonnay with a brief mention of aromatic white wines and thus didn't answer the question with sufficient breadth. The main issue however seemed to be technical misunderstandings. Not only were the bacteria involved a confusion for candidates but also the basic science of MLF. pH levels were all over the place and either rose or fell after MLF. Ideal temperatures to conduct MLF also varied from ''low 12ºC'' to "high 36ºC". 5.

commentary: What are the winemaker's options and challenges in colour management for different wine styles? Key Understanding: - A broad essay inviting the candidate to demonstrate their knowledge of a wide variety of process options and the core relationship between colour and skins. The inter-related notions of tannin management and also pH and wine stability are critical. Spoilage factors from rot- related colour destabilization through to oxidation - deliberate or accidental - post fermentation should also have been addressed. Despite being a large topic area with many different areas to address, this should have been a relatively straightforward question to approach. As with all large, open questions where there is the temptation to write too much, a good, clear introduction is necessary. A well-structured introduction lays out the map for answering the question - candidates who have one generally stand a good chance of passing. Paper 2 answers generally benefit from using the natural structure and 12 chronology of the winemaking process as a basis for their structure - for the Examiner it is logical and easy to follow and shows an organised pattern of thinking. It also helps the candidate identify areas of interest that might easily be forgotten under the pressure of the Exam. Most candidates seemed comfortable covering colour extraction techniques in different winemaking styles, but a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only. Others used statements like "high temperatures" and "longer time" - more specific, factual insight was required. Candidates also often failed to mention, or showed poor understanding of, winemaking processes post-fermentation, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak) and fining, as well as the role of oxygen. The best answers covered at least a few of these areas, giving a much more complete answer to the question. With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example. Passing answers normally have a good tempo and a logical flow - and the Examiner should of course never be questioning a candidate's technical knowledge or assumptions about winemaking practices. 6.

commentary: Examine the pros and cons of skin contact during the winemaking process. Key Understanding: Although the question seems straightforward, it is very important to clarify how it will be approached. Candidates must provide a useful definition of skin contact and should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified). Candidates should demonstrate a good understanding of the processes involved with each wine colour and style and use examples from around the world to support their statements. The question can thus be approached either through each category of wine or by the various outcomes that will be affected by skin contact. A similar style question to the previous one, answered perhaps slightly better with a handful of good passes. Also quite similar to a question from last year's Exam so perhaps candidates were well prepared for this very topical area. As per the previous question, failure often resulted because of poor structure or incomplete answers that failed to address major winemaking styles (red, rosé, white etc). While it can be useful to clearly state the areas you will address in your answer it is not acceptable to state that you will omit areas like red winemaking because all red wines have skin contact. There is definitely a trend for candidates to list all they know about a topic area as a form of answer - this will rarely pass, or producing a load of examples with no context or argument linking them. Time and again the one thing that appears lacking is evidence of original thinking, or critical analysis. Few candidates are able to present examples in a way that shows there are different ways to the same solution (e.g. winemaker 1 does A to arrive at C, while winemaker 2 does B to arrive at C) or that one can use the same techniques to arrive at different outcomes (e.g. winemaker 1 punches down because they like gentle tannin extraction, while winemaker 2 punches down to achieve full extraction). In this way the candidate can demonstrate that the world of wine is complex and subjective, highly localised and global, and ever changing - and that they understand it. 13 A number of introductions end with sentences like, 'This essay will examine…' and then repeat the question, failing to refer the Examiner to what the candidate intends to write and conveys a lack of mastery or flow on the topic. Good, passing answers are detailed but do not waste words or repeat them. Good (but all too few) answers to this question broached summary concepts, for instance that all wines experience an element of skin contact, or that there has been a trend in the past 10 years to aim for more extraction on whites and less extraction on reds. Such answers showed understanding as well as knowledge, covering a range of skin contact methods and their risks. 14

question_text: What are the most common causes of bacterial spoilage in wine? What effect do they each have, and what measures can be employed to guard against them? Your answer may consider the whole grape growing and winemaking process.
paper_preamble: 2016 MW Theory Exam Paper Three - Examiners' Report Caroline Gilby MW General comments As ever, failure to answer the question was a common complaint by Examiners, though they did comment favourably on improved use of examples compared to previous years. However, examples alone don't answer the questions but must be used to support reasoning. Another comment from Examiners was that over-long introductions rarely gain more marks. Candidates would be better simply summarising their understanding of the question and ground to be covered, and then move on to the body of the answer. Lack of attention to answering the question and drifting off topic was a widespread issue and a strong but concise introduction would help candidates focus. Paper 3 is a technical paper and it is expected that candidates will have a firm grasp of some key technical information. EU limits for SO2 use, typical levels of free SO2, actual values for pH, permitted and actual usage levels for other additives, pore sizes for filtration and so on are key knowledge for MWs. Vague comments like "lower levels of SO2" are not sufficient - actual numbers are required. Inaccurate use of "Sulphur" instead of sulphites or sulphur dioxide still crops up regularly. Candidates need to allow time to do a sense check on numbers stated too - 50mg of molecular SO2 or SO2 in grammes per litre both undermine Examiners' confidence in a candidate's understanding. 1.

commentary: What are the most common causes of bacterial spoilage in wine? What effect do they each have, and what measures can be employed to guard against them? Your answer may consider the whole grape growing and winemaking process. A very varied standard of answers with marks ranging from 20s to high 70s. This showed that the question could be answered well. However far too many candidates seemed unaware of the difference between bacteria and fungi (different kingdoms of life!) and wasted time talking about Brettanomyces and yeast. Some even believed that TCA, reduction, mildew and botrytis were bacterial issues. A definition of "spoilage" would have been useful here as too many talked about general microbial issues in the vineyards and wasted time rather than focusing on the negative effect on the wine itself. Acetobacter and LAB were the main issues to be covered here but several candidates failed to mention LAB and thus could not gain good marks if ignoring approximately half the required coverage. Some technical and numerical detail was essential here to gain good marks. 2.

commentary: What should a winemaker's main considerations be when preparing a finished wine for bottling? This question provided the highest pass rate on this paper, perhaps because it could be answered well by covering practical aspects and using examples rather than having to show high levels of technical understanding. This was quite a broad question so it was important that candidate did show adequate breadth of knowledge. Many candidates simply failed to cover enough ground - the answer needed to cover 15 wine stability but also legal conformity and chemical analysis, and many answers only did part of this. SO2 was generally well covered (though not knowing legal limits is disappointing in an MW candidate) but understanding of the use of other additives was less good. The question was on preparing a finished wine for bottling, rather than preparing the bottling line: some candidates focused on line hygiene or packaging and didn't expand on the thinking around the wine. commentary: Consider the key issues for storage of wine after packing is complete. What should have been a relatively straightforward question to answer wasn't the case. This question had the lowest pass mark of this paper but some candidates scored over 70% so it certainly wasn't impossible! Many of the candidates went off on a tangent and focused on areas not relevant to the question - transport was a common distraction. A considerable number merely made statements without getting into any depth of discussion or detail to show to the Examiner that they understood not just the question but also the key point that they were making. As a result, a number of the essays rambled when they needed to be more succinct. In an essay like this it was perhaps not easy to find examples and this proved to be the case with many candidates not providing sufficient real evidence to support their point of view. 4.

Unfortunately, that meant candidates did need to understand all three parts of the question to gain high marks, though answers could be quite concise. question_text: Who is making money in the wine industry and why? Discuss in detail three specific examples of profitable wine businesses from different parts of the wine industry supply chain.
paper_preamble: 2016 MW Theory Exam Paper Four - Examiners' Report Simon Thorpe MW General comments Despite a good overall pass rate of approximately 30%, this year we saw an increased number of candidates who were competent at producing a technically sound set of answers for this paper, but who lacked a sufficient depth of knowledge and insight to demonstrate the required level to become an MW. Equally this year, we saw a larger number of candidates who produced one good answer but were less successful in the other two. The key point is that we require "understanding" of the subject matter and the context within which wine is commercialised, rather than simply a re- iteration of theory with a prescribed set of examples. The other major concern is the lack of data and empirical evidence to support arguments. There were many answers with no factual evidence; this is a commercial paper and it is simply not possible to answer successfully without detailed analysis and real life examples. As stated in previous years, it is vitally important to be consistent with the time allocated to each of the three questions; no short or excessively long, rambling answers. Having said that, there is always a place for concise, clear answers with apposite examples or for an original way of approaching a question. 1.

commentary: Who is making money in the wine industry and why? Discuss in detail three specific examples of profitable wine businesses from different parts of the wine industry supply chain. This question was attempted by the majority of candidates. With a question that, to a large extent, defined the structure of the answer, Examiners were looking for high quality insight into businesses in the different parts of the supply chain. Simply put, those who could demonstrate that insight did well, those that couldn't didn't. We needed numbers, profit, margins, ROI, not theory or a list of companies that have been perceived to be profitable. Perhaps the biggest challenge lay in keeping this succinct - a number of candidates failed this question (and probably suffered in time management as a result). One thing to bear in mind is that examples need to be accurate as such a factual and empirical paper can be checked for accuracy! 2.

commentary: What is a "virtual winery"? Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of this business model. An uncomplicated question, but not very popular with only 21 responses. Those that did answer were generally successful, with the highest pass rate at approaching 60%. Clearly this is an 17 increasing type of business model, and becoming more and more relevant, despite growing consumer demand for provenance and product authenticity. The strengths and weaknesses are fairly standard, and structurally this is not a challenging question; hence the high pass rate. This is purely about understanding the pros and cons, both from a financial and marketing/brand building perspective as well as the pragmatics. Having good, personal examples is a massive help. Poorer answers were too superficial and lacked context. 4.

commentary: What are the most quantifiable signs that a wine brand is strong? A popular question, and seemingly fairly straightforward, but in fact this received the lowest average mark and the lowest pass rate. This needed the candidates to apply their own structure, and this is where a lot fell short. The Examiners' comments are littered with "lack of structure", "wandering", "starts well then meanders". There were really very few excellent answers here and no doubt the key word was "quantifiable". This surely points towards the metrics/measurable elements of brand evaluation. All too often this just became a list of strong brands - not at all what the question was looking for. Candidates should seek out brand owners and ask what they measure to gauge the progress of their brands and the marketing teams of those brand owners to see what they look for on a Monday morning. 5.

It would have been very difficult to approach this question without facts and figures in the first half and an opinion in the second. However we were surprised that this was not very well answered, and there were a great many confused, superficial or errant answers. This is a commercial paper, the question refers to commercial, but too often answers strayed into the technical pros and cons. In the second half of the question, it is perfectly acceptable, or even desired, to come down on one side or the other. There cannot be a correct empirical answer to this, so it is an opportunity to show some assertiveness. There were plenty of factual errors here as well, which were easily discovered when checked. 18

question_text: "The consumer's limited knowledge is a blessing for the wine industry." Discuss.
paper_preamble: 2016 MW Theory Exam Paper Five - Examiners' Report Beverley Blanning MW General comments Paper 5 is, perhaps more than any other paper, a test of written communication skills. It aims to give aspiring MWs the ability to communicate their own ideas, insights and knowledge of contemporary issues that affect the wine industry today. The Examiners are looking for evidence of analysis and independent thought, as well as the ability to construct an argument with conviction and authority. The general quality of essay writing was good, with very few poor candidates. A few candidates let themselves down with very basic spelling errors of wine terms or names. Many more promising candidates failed to pass because they did not answer the specific question on the paper. The importance of this cannot be over stressed. Writing a good, or even very good, general essay on the topic will not pass if it fails to address the exact question asked. It is recommended that students spend time analysing the question from all angles and planning their answers before starting to write. Success in this paper depends largely on addressing the issues raised in the questions fully to demonstrate depth and breadth of knowledge. As far as content goes, any argument made must be balanced by demonstrating understanding of the opposing view; personal opinion is often sought, but it needs to be backed up by credible arguments; and any question asking the student to 'discuss' requires a balanced consideration of both sides of the question. 1. commentary: The consumer's limited knowledge is a blessing for the wine industry." Discuss. This was the more popular of the two questions in the first section, but many candidates were let down by their failure to answer the question. There were two main issues here. First, 'Discuss' requires students to argue the proposition from both sides. A very one-sided approach is highly unlikely to provide enough convincing evidence for a pass grade. Another problem was that a number of students failed to spot that the question asked for discussion of consumers' limited knowledge from the perspective of the wine industry and therefore needed to be answered from the point of view of the wine industry, not the consumer. There was plenty of material to cover, including analysis of different sectors of the wine industry (from producers to retailers, educators and journalists) and different types of consumer. Candidates needed to take a broad approach in order to show their understanding of the issues involved. Limited knowledge implies scope for education, influence and marketing Candidates needed to show appreciation of the long- and short-term effects of limited consumer knowledge. 2.

commentary: How much should a consumer trust the words of a wine commentator? This was a question that allowed plenty of room for individual interpretation and opinion. However, certain elements were key to a successful answer. Candidates needed to identify that there are many different types of wine commentator (from bloggers and journalists to sommeliers, retail staff 19 and so on) and also different types of consumer (from complete novice to trade professional). Many candidates defined these terms too narrowly, with the result that their answers were insufficiently comprehensive to warrant a pass. We were looking for a nuanced understanding of the trustworthiness of wine commentators based on, for example, their reputation, financial incentives, who they write or speak for, their relevance to the consumer, links to producers, etc. The wording of the question required an opinion from the candidate. This was another area that seemed problematic for many: either no opinion was forthcoming, or it was not convincingly argued. Any opinion needs to be supported, demonstrating understanding of alternative points of view and backed by facts wherever possible. 3.

commentary: Which is more important in wine: tradition or innovation? This was by far the most popular question in section B. Candidates needed to show understanding of the definitions of and differences between tradition and innovation, and how they relate specifically to wine. To answer the question successfully it was necessary to write about both tradition and innovation and not, as many students did, choose one (invariably innovation) at the expense of the other. This approach gave rather simplistic answers that lacked the information to address the nub of the question. The best answers discussed the dynamics and continuum between tradition and innovation, showing an awareness of historical context and using examples to show that both are important for wine. There were many ways to approach this question. Candidates could have explored the notion of innovations becoming traditions, or traditions in one region being adopted as innovations in another. Discussion of 'important' could be considered in terms of wine styles, consumers, producers, cultural heritage, or uniqueness. The best papers examined the question in the context of the entire chain from the land to the end user. 4.

Answers generally showed a good grasp of the subject, but few excelled. 20

question_text: Temperature is one of the most impactful environmental variables on wine grape growing. How does temperature affect viticulture?
paper_preamble: Paper 1 report Joel Butler MW General Comments The range of questions for this year's Paper 1 covered the core syllabus and a number of issues and interests that the examiners believe are topical. Three questions of the six presented clearly required consideration of climate/climate change to gain a passing mark. Half of the questions posed (Q1,Q3,Q6) concerned globally important issues, requiring careful reading of the question, analysis with global examples, and an awareness of the need to focus on the main thrust of the question. Examiners observed that overall, a solid majority of candidates showed solid knowledge about a given question, but noted that there were still papers which a) failed to define well the parameters of their discussion based upon the terms of the question; b) failed to answer both parts of a question; c) made inaccurate factual statements; d) answered questions too generally and with inadequate, generic examples. Although the average marks for all questions was a solid "C", the overall pass rate this year was less than in 2016. The Examiners suggest three areas for concern. The first is lack of knowledge about current viticultural procedures, timing and key concerns, globally. The second is not reading questions carefully and writing descriptive rather than analytical answers, effectively answering a different question(s) than asked. Thirdly, Examiners noted a number of papers that were short and lacking content, indicating possible time management issues. 1.
theory_chair_report: Theory Panel Chair Report Neil Tully MW This year's theory exam produced 35 full theory passes, representing a 32.7% pass rate (2016 = 28.9%) and one single paper re-sit. There were a good number of very strong, and indeed, a number of exceptional theory papers which were a joy to read. Well-prepared candidates writing with authority and conviction, at all times keeping their responses closely tailored to the question, achieved some excellent marks. In contrast to the uneven performance of many candidates in last year's theory exam, this year the majority of candidates performed much more evenly across the five theory papers. This is an encouraging sign. There were also fewer cases of candidates running out of time on their last question. We also saw significantly fewer "All I know about" type essay responses, which is welcome. Specific detail for each of the theory papers is contained within the Paper Chairs' examiners' reports, but a number of common themes have emerged which warrant comment here. Less successful responses often lost focus. Precision of expression reflects precision of thought. Never lose sight of the question, and do pay careful attention to the way the question is worded. A few otherwise strong responses lost marks where the question was either misinterpreted, or only partially answered. The words used in the question are very carefully considered, nothing is accidental, and often indicate the anticipated structure of the response. Do be sure to use technical terms accurately. Misused terminology undermines the credibility of your response. Many candidates would have benefitted from reading through their finished responses and checking them before finishing the exam. Time should be allowed to do this; many errors and omissions which might have resulted from "exam pressure" could have been corrected, extra marks gained, and importantly, credibility in the eyes of the examiners would have been restored. An essay peppered with careless typing errors does not reflect the expected level of professionalism. The examiners would like to point out that the use of the "smiley face", though entertaining, is not considered appropriate in an MW exam essay ;-( Theory
commentary: Temperature is one of the most impactful environmental variables on wine grape growing. How does temperature affect viticulture? A successful response to this question required addressing the statement in the first sentence as well as the question in the second sentence. The first sentence certainly required some definition or explanation of the phrase "most impactful". Good papers summed up temperature's impact on the vineyard nicely in one paragraph. But the actual question in the second sentence seemed misunderstood by several candidates. Indeed, as one examiner noted about one answer: "…more a discourse on how climate affects vineyards at different points, with too few relevant connections to actual responses in the vineyard to temperature/climate issues." This question sought the ability to connect temperature variability to specific practices in the vineyard, relative to the type of wine or grape varieties produced. This question was not about climate change per se (though good answers addressed that issue in a coherent manner). Examiners noted instances of what seemed like a stock response on climate change, without any attempt to tie it in to the question. Passing papers correctly made the connection between practical responses in the vineyard during the year to temperature-driven situations in different wine growing climate zones. Some papers revealed a lack of 'real-world' understanding of how to respond viticulturally to the seasonal variations in a vineyard brought on by temperature, engaging examples from books rather than from concrete examples reflecting direct experience or communication with producers around the world. Simple factual errors are now less common, examiners noted. However, in some cases confidence was undermined by ignorance of, for example, the lack of knowledge of relevant temperatures and timings which might cause plant growth to stop, the forthcoming crop to be lost or the death of the whole plant. Examiners were pleased to see (in the words of one Examiner) "nice global knowledge, and ties to the question, and …understands the key issues." Important issues that could have been considered and discussed (with the necessary viticultural responses) for a passing paper included: temperature variability, individual varietal tolerance to low and high temperatures, temperatures needed for ripening a balanced crop, air and soil temperatures, warmer and colder soil structures and their effects, the influence of humidity and possible climate change effects on individual grape varieties. 2.

commentary: candidate. 3. Labour supply for vineyard work is decreasing in many parts of the world. If this trend continues, how will this affect viticulture, and how can vineyard managers around the world best prepare for, and handle, a shortage of workers? This question had the greatest number of responses on Paper 1. The inclination might have been to answer it as a Paper 4 (business of wine) question. Indeed this happened frequently and accordingly the pass rate for this question was the lowest on the Paper. The question required global consideration of labour availability relative to the needs of producers to maintain profitability. Conditions might range from more restrictive US immigration of Latin American farmhands to the inability to rely on workers in war-torn areas owing to their migration to nearby wine-growing areas such as Lebanon. Above all, a good paper had to consider how mechanisation can provide solutions across a spectrum of viticultural needs to alleviate a shrinking labour supply. A strong response may have included how to better manage labour year-round, for example by providing education and training to perform a range of vineyard tasks by a smaller group of permanent workers. Passing papers overall reflected what one Examiner noted: "Good examples and demonstrating knowledge in key areas of mechanisation plus sufficient discussion on training and multi-discipline approach to work." Summing up, a passing answer acknowledged and discussed the various viticultural tasks (across the life of the vineyard from establishment to grubbing up, as well as during the grape/wine growing year) that can be automated or mechanised, as well as those that cannot. 4.

commentary: Discuss which vine varieties would be most suitable for the production of dessert wines. Explain your choice with specific reference to any climatic requirements. This question called for a good demonstration of candidates' global experience and knowledge. It required a range of viticulture practices to be considered within a framework of options that address the climate requirements for the production of dessert wine styles. To earn a passing mark, it was vital not to ignore fortified wine. It was also critical to understand "dessert" wine as a wine with the assumption of sweetness, and an awareness of the levels of sweetness across a wide range of varieties and wine styles. Finally, remembering this was a Paper 1 question, good answers clearly linked variety and style of wine to its climate requirements. This included choice of variety based upon criteria such as skin thickness, rate of sugar accumulation, acidity and aromatic compound levels, production method, and humidity levels. The best papers noted that the relationship between climatic requirements and varieties flowed in both directions; that is, varieties adapting to their climate niche over time (Semillon in Sauternes) or climate requirements dictating adaptation of a particular grape variety based upon the unique production methods necessary (PX in Montilla-Moriles). Most papers answered the first part of the question well enough, but the link to the climatic requirements sometimes broke down. There was overall, good discussion of various varieties and why they made for good dessert wines. Sometimes, however, that discussion didn't reflect enough consideration of the many viticultural reasons why they were ideal dessert wine grapes. Examiners noted that several papers merely 'surveyed' the varietal scene for dessert wines, but made no attempt to answer the question. The huge global choice of wines/varieties to discuss necessitated making choice about 'the most suitable' varieties to discuss as the question demanded. For example, several papers were convincing regarding varieties, botrytis influence and the connected climatic issues, but some erred, citing Furmint, Semillon, Riesling and Chenin Blanc as all successful due to their thin skins. Top marks went to those papers that strongly linked a variety's characteristics to the climatic considerations that made it the right choice for that place, and for the method of production best suited to expressing character. One Examiner noted, "As we know, dessert wines can come from many diverse climates, and the weather conditions from vintage to vintage often stray beyond the 'norm'. But to try to grapple with both those variables at once in an essay this short was very tough." Therefore the examiners tried to be flexible and generous in marking, so long as factual errors were absent, and most of the categories (still, fortified etc) were considered in the discussion with relevant examples. 5.

commentary: Does soil preparation affect the potential yield and quality in a vineyard? Question 5 prompted the fewest responses (34) on Paper 1, perhaps reflecting a lack of knowledge by candidates of this important viticultural activity, or perhaps because many felt intimidated by the rhetorical nature of the question. The Examiners noted this question as one requiring sound knowledge of viticulture to answer well. The question asked the writer to address the role played by the soil when it comes to providing support for the vine throughout its life cycle, its ability to provide the vine with water, and physical support for the vine. Candidates were asked to consider the various options available to vineyard managers when it comes to soil preparation, and importantly the impact of these interventions on yield and quality. Several papers answered a different question in their authors' minds, along the lines of "Describe everything you know about why soil is important". Issues such as annual pre- season preparation or biodynamic preparations also fell within the scope of this question. It was critical to understand that Soil Preparation encompasses major physical steps such as ripping, weed control and soil pH adjustment, as well as major "chemical" steps such as addition of nutrients such as Potassium or Nitrogen; about why, how and when these should be done and the effect on quality and yield. Equally important was the issue of water availability and the physical support requirements of the soil for vines and then referencing the different means of preparation relative to the type of wine being produced, be it Château Latour or Pinot Grigio del Veneto. Global examples were critical to obtaining a good pass. Successful papers included discussion of established vineyards, as well as commentary about new technologies now used to help with soil preparation. A number of otherwise solid papers covered physical preparation in detail, but omitted nutrient and water issues. Examiners did note that with a question like this one, not identifying "experts" did weaken an argument. 6.

commentary: What are the principal pests and diseases facing vine growers today, and how can they best be managed? A popular question and the most successfully answered overall. Critical to answering it well was defining 'principal', 'pests and diseases', and 'manage'. If one didn't do some form of triage and focus on those that are 'principal' around the world today, and knowing what to do about them, it was very easy to "not see the wood for the trees". Examiners are aware of the sheer number of issues affecting vine-growers globally, and thus set a broad range of pests and diseases that could be considered, giving candidates the opportunity to focus on 7-8 of which they considered important. This was a question in which the best papers clearly highlighted the writer's real experience due to direct knowledge from producers, and demonstrated their global awareness of the situation. Good passing papers considered the differences between physical pests such as deer, and those pests transmitting diseases: nematodes, leafhoppers, mites, mealybugs. Likewise, it was critical to discuss (and distinguish) between key bacterial/fungal diseases such as Pierce's Disease, Flavescence Dorée, botrytis, Eutypa, Esca, and viral ones such as fan leaf virus, red blotch and leafroll. The key to a pass here was clearly presenting arguments and examples demonstrating an understanding of managing and controlling the said disease. In the words of one Examiner commenting on a particularly good paper: "A very detailed answer, well organised and peppered with relevant examples. It defined 'principle' or how the pests/diseases discussed were selected, considers costs and considered biodynamic/organic treatments as well. It mentioned most of the pests and diseases, and detailed how they could be curtailed." Many papers (not all!) nominated phylloxera as (still) a principal pest. So long as the discussion of management was relatively short and pointed out that it is not a significant threat in most places due to better knowledge, examiners were positive in their marking consideration. Discussions of management needed to consider varying growing conditions and the philosophy of the producer; the best papers confidently discussed management options open to organic/biodynamic growers as well as the less restrictive ones available to more conventional growers.

question_text: "This wine has been bottled un-fined and unfiltered." Assess the implications for the winemaker.
paper_preamble: Theory Paper 2 Report Meg Brodtmann MW General Comments The Paper 2 Examiners made the same general comments that they have made every year and these are bullet pointed below to ensure they are clear. • Paper 2 is a technical paper and you cannot pass without including technical details! • Spelling. If a candidate cannot spell wine regions, winemaking terms etc., it does not imbue much confidence in the examiner. One of the key aspects of the MW is communication and you cannot communicate with poor spelling. • Answer the question! Do not brain-dump to fill the paper with words. • Listing examples that are out of date indicate that the student is not aware of the current state of the industry. Examples must be relevant, global, varied and support the argument rather than be used as the argument. • If you are not sure of the facts, don´t put them in. • Do not just focus on the premium end of production, students should also understand how large volume wines are made. • Too many students use the technique of saying "who does what where" but do not show any critical thinking. This is linked to brain dumping but we are invariably asking you to take a position and critically apply your knowledge. • Handwriting needs to be legible. • Do not use derogatory terms or make harsh judgement calls on wine styles, regions, etc - the winemaker may be marking your paper! 1. commentary: This wine has been bottled unfined and unfiltered'. Assess the implications for the winemaker. A question that tested candidates' knowledge of what procedures are available, what is legal in different parts of the world, what the difference is between fining and filtration (which wasn't always clearly addressed!) and - crucially - what other winery activities can be undertaken, or are implied, if fining and filtration are forsaken. The major over-riding omission was the simple failure to talk about how things like yields, sulphur dioxide regime and vat/barrel ageing might be deployed to achieve greater stability and clarity in the absence of fining and filtering. The more successful responses to this question looked at the whole range of winemaking procedures that can be employed to eliminate the need for fining and filtration. Confusion over the difference between fining and filtration was also quite surprising - candidates must have clear definitions of these two processes before starting a question such as this. Quite a few candidates preferred to consider the labelling and marketing implications of what might be considered bad winemaking rather than the technicalities of winemaking, which is what this paper is about. It also seemed difficult for students to discuss the implications for the winemaker of making unfined and unfiltered wine. A list of who is doing what, as opposed to a technical approach, is not enough. 2.

commentary: Sauvignon Blanc appears in many styles throughout the world. Compare and contrast Sauvignon Blanc winemaking practices around the world. Some excellent responses to this question showed good knowledge and understanding and got to the essence of why wines are different from the same variety and how, with a variety such as Sauvignon Blanc, a winemaker can embrace a great many options if they have the knowledge, skill and the courage to step away from a mainstream trend. Candidates should however beware of overgeneralisation. The examiners commented on the very frequent reference to only a few examples, for example Fumé Blanc in the USA without considering newer producers who are making complex Sauvignon Blanc in that country. Examiners were looking for a discussion of reductive versus oxidative winemaking, use of expressive yeasts, use of oak, international examples and blending. The candidates needed to back up their comments with sound technical information. A small number of essays gave welcome thought to technical winemaking such as separating press fractions, types of fining practices, how residual sugar may be employed, and stabilisation. Some less well prepared candidates tended to waffle and focus almost solely on high quality, terroir-driven wines while neglecting the presence of high volume wines. This question gave the candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their reasoning with use of international examples to support their arguments. Few took this opportunity. It also gave the candidates a great opportunity to cover off a lot of winemaking practices in one essay. 3.

commentary: Discuss the role of enzymes in winemaking. This was one of the less popular questions on this year's theory paper two. However, a competent candidate had the ability to really shine here and get high marks whereas those candidates that were less confident on the subject found this question extremely challenging. This was reflected in the marks achieved - good passes or clear fails with very little in between. Those candidates that did not do well failed to define what an enzyme is and what it does. Like so many other essays, candidates should have started at the beginning of the winemaking process and worked their way through discussing the use of enzymes at the various steps and stages. Candidates needed to discuss red, white and rosé winemaking. It was interesting to note how few candidates mentioned enzymes and red winemaking, demonstrating a big, general gap in knowledge. Commercial enzyme types were mostly covered but few, if any, candidates discussed spoilage enzymes present in grapes. Again, a systematic approach covering the whole winemaking process would allow candidates a structure on which to hang their points. 4.

commentary: Compare and contrast winemaking techniques best employed for Syrah grown in Cornas, McLaren Vale and Hawke's Bay. Although few candidates attempted this question, many papers were competent with few really poor answers. This question required a good understanding of winemaking in the regions described. Clearly the students mostly understood the winemaking techniques of the Rhone/Cornas and some were conversant with McLaren Vale/or warm climate areas, but fewer were conversant with Hawke's Bay. At first this may have felt like a red wine version of Question 2. In fact, it opened up into a far greater invitation to the student to accurately describe what makes McLaren Vale distinct from other classic Australian regions such as Barossa, and what makes Cornas distinct from other classic Rhone appellations. This was a huge micro-terroir question, potentially allowing students to compare and contrast the different winemaking techniques in the three regions, and how they impact on quality and style. Very few answers addressed this, with most electing to describe McLaren Vale as if it were part of a gigantic generic Australian whole and Cornas as if it were entirely representative of all Northern Rhone reds. 5.

We urge candidates to address the question and not just tell us everything they know about a particular topic. Paper 2 is a technical paper and not only do candidates need to know the names of common yeast types involved in the winemaking process (be they good or bad!) but they also need to be able to spell the names of the yeast correctly. Narrow minded comments such as "selected yeasts only produce short lived wines"... or "Spoilage yeasts and Brett can be used to bring out terroir"… do not suggest a deep understanding. Nor do generalisations about old world and new world wine styles. Questions related to yeasts appear with some regularity so it is surprising to see candidates still failing to grasp the role of the different yeast genus and species. This is one area where much R&D is spent so students would be wise to keep themselves up to date with what is going on. It is also wise to ensure the examples used are global and relevant.

commentary: Outline the most important quality control checks during bottling and why each is necessary. Key understanding: Recognition of: • Most important risks inherent in bottling process, how and when these arise • Consequent need for and timing of quality control checks • What these checks comprise • Relevant regulation and voluntary codes relevant to quality control • Commercial consequences of failing to address these risks adequately (implicit in the wider scope of "why each [check] is necessary") Candidates should be aware that bottling (to include alternative packaging) is the final step of wine production during which the wine can be microbiologically compromised or damaged by oxygen ingress. Bottling isn't solely about putting a wine into bottle, it is also about ensuring the correct wine/variety is bottled, correct bottle type is used and the correct packaging is applied. There were few really strong answers to this question and lots of candidates lacked focus or missed too many key issues. Candidates needed to consider both quality checks on wine and checks on the packaging process and dry goods, as well as compliance with product specification. Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question, showing lack of awareness of key QC analyses for wine and why they are carried out - essential knowledge for potential MWs. Consideration of HACCP is always useful in a question that mentions bottling. Quality control is part of the overall quality assurance process and wine is a food stuff which must comply with legislative and regulatory standards (so an awareness of EU legislation and ISO requirements is helpful). A lot of candidates missed the critical "why" part of the question, and without considering this, their answers were too superficial and lacked analytical depth. The safety of staff handling the liquid and the packaging is critical (risks like broken glass, noise, heavy lifting and exposure to health risks). Issues for the wine itself include loss of quality, consumer disappointment, damage to brand, and costs attached to issuing recalls or being unable to sell the wine. 2.

commentary: What analyses should be carried out at the winery pre- and post-bottling to ensure that a wine is in good condition and conforms to legal requirements for sale? Key understanding: Key elements of the answer should show understanding of what can theoretically go wrong at the bottling stage, and how analysis can help prevent wines being bottled in poor condition and within the legal parameters. An understanding of the methods that are widely used and the legal limits for the various constituents of wine is required. This question had the highest pass rate at 50%, indicating that it was straightforward for candidates with good levels of technical knowledge. This question required knowledge of key quality control analyses establishing a wine to be in good condition, both before bottling and after. It also shows whether it is likely to remain so after the bottling process and until it reaches the consumer. Specifically, the question asked "what analyses" yet there were disappointingly few answers which listed and explained the key QC analyses and their importance in ensuring the wine's good condition and conformation to legal requirements. Several candidates simply discussed issues that might arise and not what QC checks were required. Here again the key problem was the overall lack of technical information and analytical reasoning in many of the answers. The comment "too qualitative" was used by examiners for many of the scripts. Candidates also needed to know legal limits (EU or other key markets) for key wine constituents and additives, plus allergens. Knowledge of labelling requirements was also required (e.g. sweetness declarations such as medium-dry or halbtrocken, allergens, sulphite declarations, alcohol tolerances). Supporting examples would be helpful too. 3.

commentary: Many winemakers are reducing the levels of free and total sulphites in wine. Consider the role of sulphites at bottling and until the wine reaches the end consumer. What are the implications of reduced levels of free sulphites? Key understanding:  Risks arising at bottling and continuing until wine reaches consumer.  The four distinct properties of SO2 - anti-oxidant, anti-microbial, anti-oxidasic and (less important) binding with acetaldehyde.  Focus on the role of SO2 at bottling to the end consumer and the implications of lowering the level of free sulphur dioxide - i.e. wine not being in drinkable condition or developing prematurely, or developing faults such as microbial fermentations.  The role of free and total sulphur dioxide - in various wines, including numbers.  Potential risks to health at high levels of free SO2, consumer concern about additives, especially since requirement for obligatory sulphite labelling. Lower levels may improve aromatic expression in young wines.  Natural wines made with no added sulphur dioxide, or very little. Customers for such wines may have higher tolerance for what some would see as faults. The "implications" part of the question required a definition of what "reduced levels" of free SO2 mean. A free SO2 level below 10ppm will run the risk of the wine oxidising and be a concern to the winemaker, unless it is a natural wine that is being produced. Free sulphur dioxide has a major purpose in preventing wine from oxidising both at the time of bottling (dissolved oxygen pick up) and during the life of the wine. It also helps maintain the wine's freshness plus inhibits yeast and bacteria, and thus reduces risk of refermentation in bottle (including malolactic fermentation) and these are essentially the implications of reducing the level of free sulphur dioxide at bottling. Implications in managing risks: crucial importance of aseptic state of all bottling equipment, bottles and stoppers; reduced temperature of bottling environment, storage and transit to consumer; inherent energy cost. Storage and transit after leaving producer's premises are out of producer's control and so a particular risk. It is still surprising how many candidates do not know current EU levels for total SO2, nor typical levels of free SO2 in different styles of wine, nor what constitutes lower levels in actual numbers. It is really important to have these facts committed to memory. Clarity about the difference between free and total SO2 is also important. It was clear that quite a number of otherwise good candidates misread the question: instead of addressing the "implications of reduced levels of free sulphites", they wrote about the implications for the winemaker of reducing free sulphites/how to achieve low sulphite wines. Their essays thus focused on adjustments to be made in the winemaking process, so treating it substantially as a Paper 2 question. These essays would typically score in the late 50s/early 60s but would not pass. There were, however, lots of very good scripts which did address (both parts of) the question directly and met the standard to pass. As a general comment on the answers to Q3, one examiner expressed the view that "there were many candidates who appeared either to have pre-prepared an essay on the use of SO2 and who rolled it out with disregard for the focus of the exam question or who mis-read the question; consequently there were a number of candidates who, in the abstract, appear technically knowledgeable but who have not attained a pass mark."

commentary: 4. Write concise short notes on 3 of the following topics: a) Preservatives in wine b) Preventing deposits in bottled wine c) Inert storage d) Pre-bottling filtration Key understanding: Straightforward technical answer for candidates with good knowledge base. Those candidates who failed this question usually did so because their answers were insufficiently wide and/or deep in scope in addressing the chosen topic. Writing 'short notes' still has to evidence sufficient knowledge and understanding for MW level and use supporting examples. Quite a number appear to have left this question until the end of the exam and may not have left themselves enough time to do justice to it. One examiner commented, "in contrast, there were some outstanding answers, which were a joy to read." Preservatives in wine needed to cover more than simply sulphites. Alcohol itself is significant for its preservative action and other preservatives like ascorbic acid and potassium sorbate also needed to be covered. Mention could be made of lysozyme and Velcorin for their preservative action too. The action of ascorbic acid and sorbic acid was muddled by several candidates Deposits in bottled wine was often taken to mean tartrate crystals only. Other deposits such as protein, metal casse and microbial hazes needed to be mentioned. Inert storage answers were generally sound. Filtration was well answered by some, but anecdotal and too general by others and often failed to cover anything but pre-bottling membrane filtration.
