This may well lead the candidate to take a PESTLE or SWOT approach, or alternatively to analyse the benefits/weaknesses of each element of the supply chain in turn from producer through to consumer. The title indirectly questions the role of retailers and thus leads candidates to consider 'direct to consumer' as a route to market and thus an exploration of such emerging models (this helps to explain how routes to market are changing) especially through on-line channels. (Examples might include drop-ship, market place, set up by LVMH of 'Clos 19', Chateau Margaux opening wine bar). Overall, a good pass rate of 41%. Those that didn't fare so well were generally long on describing the market and the intermediaries that act in it, but missed out on analysis of the causes and outcomes of the changes that are taking place. commentary: inherit the equivalent of US$ 10 million and want to invest in the wine industry. How would you spend your money to attract the greatest return on investment? Explain your logic. Key Understanding: This was a far-reaching question, which could be interpreted in many different ways. It therefore required a strong, supportive structure to avoid drifting. Return on investment (ROI) needed a clear definition and a consideration of short, medium and long term horizons for accurate assessment. The risk was that candidates drifted and wrote too much, or veered off subject and wrote about a specific opportunity without considering wider options and context. (Fine to ultimately conclude on one opportunity but some broader perspective should have been given). Logical structures went through the elements of the supply chain from producer through to retailer across different channels and different markets. Alternatively a SWOT would have kept the candidate on track and demonstrated rigour and logic in their thought process. A brave but potentially narrow approach would have been a financially driven case. Answers to this question achieved the lowest pass rate at below 20%. It was designed to test understanding of financial choices in the wine industry and there's no doubt that those candidates who were able to demonstrate that understanding were the successful ones. It's also worth noting that this is a Paper 4 question, not Paper 5, so those candidates who were too dreamy and imaginative, without the financial numbers to back up their argument, were the least successful. Any industry, even the wine industry, is founded on profit generation and this was a bald, bold question asking about financial return on investment. One further point to make is the numerical inaccuracy of examples used in many answers. If this was Paper 1 or 2 then the technical aspects of wine production (maybe g/l of RS or yields per hectare) would absolutely need to be quoted accurately - the same applies to this paper for financial details. 4.

commentary: In what ways has social media changed the marketing of wine brands over the past 10 years? Key Understanding: This is a broad question that would require as a starting point a strong definition of social media. Strong candidates will recognise that there are industry studies e.g. from 'Wine Intelligence', looking at the role of social media in wine. This could help provide an evidence-based framework for answers which may have the potential to be too subjective. A key element of this question is to consider the overall marketing of wine brands and how social media has assisted (or not) and whether more classic marketing tools still prevail. Perhaps not surprisingly, this was answered by many candidates, but the pass rate was fairly low - just under a third. The comments from the examiners praised candidates who were able to provide analysis and insight in a well-structured and focused answer whilst condemning those whose arguments were hard to follow, too long and rambling. The key factor, as is often the case, was being able to assess which structure best suited the subject. From there, it was important to ensure that all the relevant points are covered and backed up with empirical evidence. This was not a question which asked for a list of social media outcomes, but specifically how social media has impacted wine brand marketing over a period of time. 5.

commentary: You are Export Director of an established large wine company producing in excess of one million nine litre cases. Key Understanding:  Size of the wine market in China and current trend of increase. Segmentation by price band.  Structure of the importer/distributor network - single national importers or multiple regional players.  Breakdown red/white/rosé/sparkling.  How do Chinese consumers access information about wine?  Demographics. Male/female split, age group preferences.  Consumer perception/understanding of grape varieties, prime regions, dry/sweet styles.  Credit risk, Counterfeiting, Price control, Distribution channels, Language barrier. A fairly well answered paper - just over 40% passing. This question couldn't be answered well unless the candidate had a good knowledge of the Chinese market, the trends/developments in the market and crucially the risks associated. There was little point attempting to answer this without that depth of understanding and yet still quite a few gave it a stab. China is such a key factor in the business of wine these days that it must be studied in some detail - knowledge of the market would have helped in every single question in Paper 4 this year. Good answers covered the bases with good examples. Great answers added in elements of the different channels/routes to market. In general, the more detailed the knowledge, the more successful the answer. 6.

Key Understanding:  The use of Bordeaux négociant network.  En primeur.  Withdrawal from the en primeur market, e.g. Latour, releasing stock at a much later date.  Combination - some en primeur, some later releases, drip-fed into the market.  Employing one's own salesforce. Analysis of benefits against additional costs.  Appointing nominated importers in selected markets. Exclusivity or multiple importers?  Cellar-door sales. Oenotourism.  Financial grasp of the costs of distribution, and margins achieved by importers and négociants. A classic question about the most established wine market. Sadly, a pass rate less than 30%, with most of the lower marks showing a lack of awareness either of the changing environment around en primeur or of the detail of the workings of the prevailing system. Also a lot of answers focused on either one or other of the commercial and brand building standpoints, but not both. The word "today" in the question implied that you should consider the contemporary issues, comparing them with the situation in the past. Again, successful questions showed deep knowledge of the mechanics of the market, the options available, with numbers-based evidence. Brand building also needed some numbers to illustrate success or failure.

commentary: 1. What is the importance of alcohol in wine? Key understandings:  The central importance of alcohol to wine, technically and legally.  The quality and sensory importance of alcohol to different styles of wine.  The cultural importance and impact on the individual and society.  Clear recognition and communication of the positive and negative aspects of alcohol in wine. This was probably the most straightforward question on the paper, so it was surprising that the pass rate was not higher. The examiners felt that the question was not well answered, perhaps because there was a lot of ground to cover and many candidates neglected to demonstrate their understanding of significant key areas. A broad and discursive approach was needed and candidates failing to take this approach were unlikely to achieve a pass. We look for analysis, not description. However, there is a wealth of factual information on the subject that MW candidates need to have at their fingertips to answer this sort of question. We were expecting to see evidence of understanding alcohol's importance for microbial stability, preservation and longevity, the legal and tax implications, and the control of alcohol consumption by governments. Awareness and discussion of alcohol's contribution to structure, balance and style, and the importance of its interaction with other elements in wine were also essential components of a good essay. A number of candidates focused almost exclusively on the health aspects of alcohol in wine, which could certainly form part of a good answer, but would have been insufficient to ensure a pass. There were many bland and over-general answers that showed neither critical thinking nor the breadth of knowledge we were looking for. 2.

commentary: Has science taken away the romance of wine? Key understandings:  The question concerns the juxtaposition of science and art: should one or other be dominant? Can they co-exist?  Understanding of romantic notions of wine, past and present.  The role of scientific developments in changing perceptions about wine. The question required candidates to consider both science and romance as they relate to wine. It was imperative to consider both sides of the question, rather than present a one-sided argument. The latter approach was taken by quite a number of unsuccessful candidates. Romance may refer to any number of intangibles, such as the mystical origins of wine, current notions of glamour and exoticism, attitudes to artisanal production, unpredictability of harvests, and so on. Candidates needed to consider for whom science may or may not have taken away the romance of wine: producers, consumers, distributors, etc. A mass-produced, scientifically-driven brand may still have romantic associations for the end consumer, for example. Arguments agreeing with the question could have been that there now are fewer unknowns in wine since much has been explained by science (fermentation, mlf, etc), or that there is no romance in 'recipe' wines, high-volume brands, or controlled winemaking. Arguments against the question could have included the fact that most consumers still have no idea how wine is really made and love to retain the romantic associations they have. Many aspects of terroir remain unknown, and how wine ages is still largely a mystery. There will always be romance when a wine is associated with special birthdays or historical events. Perhaps the revival in interest in 'authenticity' has brought back the romantic notion of wine as being a pure product of the soil, and less controlled by science. Very few candidates considered a broad definition of romance and struggled to come up with sufficient material for a convincing argument. The examiners commented that this is the type of question that demonstrates the importance of good essay writing. Many answers lacked structure. Some candidates used headings and bullet points, which rarely work in candidates' favour on this paper. 3.

commentary: How relevant is blind tasting in assessing wine? Key understandings:  The relevance of blind tasting to different groups: consumers, buyers, other wine professionals, producers, journalists, judges, etc.  The absolute usefulness and limitations of blind tasting This was another straightforward question that nevertheless tripped up a good portion of candidates who neglected to discuss the relevance of blind tasting, and instead simply listed the pros and cons. Those who did answer the question, however, generally scored well, and this question had the highest pass rate of the paper. We were looking for a thorough exploration of the practice, usefulness and limitations of blind tasting, and many candidates provided this, although surprisingly few used the example of their recent experience of the MW practical exam to illustrate their answer. 4.

commentary: What are the causes for optimism in the wine world today? Key understandings:  Ability to look at the multifaceted nature of the world of wine and identify current or upcoming elements within it that could lead to beneficial outcomes for consumer, producers and intermediaries.  Evidence of widespread global knowledge of various aspects of the world of wine.  Personal insight and ability to comment on future trends based on the current situation. This question gave candidates the opportunity to show personal insights and speculate on current trends, events and possibilities that might generate positive outcomes for any area of the wine world. Examples of causes for optimism could be: people drinking less, but better; booming wine education; a new generation valuing authenticity, thus encouraging greater sustainability in farming; greater awareness of the effects of agrochemicals, leading to cleaner wines and less polluted vineyards; the boom in craft beer with positive knock-on effects for the wine industry; new and untapped markets to exploit; positive research into wine's health benefits; the huge variety of wine available world-wide; the benefits of technology in creating reliable, high-quality product on a large scale; the possibility of growing vines in new places; the internet shifting power of information distribution to the end user, making for better informed consumers; new marketing possibilities in the digital age; wine preservation inventions increasing by-the-glass offerings; and many more. There was plenty of scope for choice of material here and this was reflected in a good number of sound passes. The candidates who fell down usually did so because of simplistic arguments that were considered below MW standard, or factual errors. A number of candidates failed because they did not answer the question and gave reasons for pessimism instead of optimism. While it could have been a valid approach to the question to argue that there are zero causes for optimism in the wine world, this would have been a position that needed justification within the context of the question. 5.

commentary: Does great wine need a great story? Key understandings:  The role of stories in communicating about wine.  What wine means to different people: from those who sell, make, buy, or drink it. This was not a popular question and the least well answered on the paper. Most candidates appeared to be unsure how to define 'great wine', so avoided doing so, which led to muddled answers that failed to reach a clear conclusion. The question was whether a great wine - however it is defined - needs a great story. In other words, is the story intrinsic to its greatness, or its perception as such? Questions that could have been addressed were: Can a great wine exist in a vacuum of information? Do those who sell, buy and drink it need more than simply the product? Do great wines make their own stories by virtue of their greatness? Is it necessary to know what a wine is (its history, provenance, etc) in order to appreciate it to the full? Would a great wine be as appreciated blind, or without its story? Are there any examples of great wines with no story? Or a wine made great by its story? Is the story only relevant for marketing, or is it intrinsic to the wine? While there was scope for differing definitions of 'great' (from high-end fine wine to globally successful brands), there needed to be some definition and an underlying logic supported by examples. Some essays appeared to consider any wine to be 'great', which made it difficult to then come up with a convincing argument that answered the question. The examiners commented that essay style let many candidates down. The best answers showed clarity and focus, using examples to good effect.

question_text: Many wine regions can produce wines at a wide range of price points. Referencing at least two of such regions, compare and contrast methods of managing vineyards for high priced wines and low priced wines.
paper_preamble: Theory Paper 1 focused on some of the key viticulture issues facing the global wine industry. The Paper also asked candidates to consider current and changing roles for viticultural practices such as pruning and whether or not old vines are worth the trouble on a practical level. Several of the themes, such as pruning and the issue of trunk diseases, were set to test candidates' grasp of real-world technical issues and scientific aspects that vine growers globally must reckon with daily. As has been repeatedly noted, Paper 1 requires a sound knowledge, technical understanding and practical application of that knowledge with appropriate examples in order to pass. Examiners noticed this year a number of papers which cited arguments from specific writers/authorities without, however, noting where the opinion or comment came from. Question 1:
theory_chair_report: Theory Panel Chair Report Neil Tully MW This year's theory exam produced 30 full theory passes, representing a 31.25% pass rate (2017 = 32.7%), and two single paper re-sits. These results demonstrate that a good number of candidates in this year's theory exam came into the exam room with an appropriate level of knowledge and understanding and, importantly, knew how to deploy that knowledge to good effect in response to the questions set. Many of the unsuccessful candidates, whilst perhaps having the necessary knowledge, were unable to use it effectively. Candidates would be well advised to gauge the level of depth and detail required for a successful response to a question at MW level. Many of the questions set could have been answered in a superficial manner with a basic level of detail, but the MW exam does require a certain precision and insight, of which candidates should be very conscious. In combination with an appropriate level of depth and detail, examiners are also looking for evidence of analytical thought. Very often, simply repeating processes or procedures will not suffice. Equally an overabundance of examples can sometimes mask a lack of fundamental understanding. Examiners across all theory papers this year commented on the repeated use of a limited number of examples. On theory paper 2, one examiner noted 21 out of 56 papers using the same reference to Domaine Dujac. While it is not unsurprising that material from seminars may be widely cited, it does not indicate a broad frame of reference. While the more commonly used examples may for very good reasons be seen as "go to" examples, examples taken from a candidate's own experience and enquiry, used appropriately, will stand out all the more. However, a word of caution; when using examples over-familiarity, even if those individuals being cited are well-known to the candidate, does not strike a suitable tone: "At Churton in Marlborough, Sam will decide to include stems…", and in another example: "According to Mike, the perceived benefit of inclusion of stems…". It should be emphasised that those candidates whose first language is not English, and who are not extremely comfortable writing in English, should seriously consider writing in their native language. In summary, candidates looking to elevate their marks would be well advised to consider first whether they are writing with an appropriate level of depth and detail, secondly whether they are showing evidence of critical analysis. This should all be conveyed in a suitable tone, and underpinned with appropriately chosen examples. 9 3i. Theory Paper One Joel Butler MW General Comments This year's
commentary: Many wine regions can produce wine at a wide range of price points. Referencing at least two of such regions, compare and contrast methods of managing vineyards for high priced wines and low priced wines. This question allowed for wide discussion, a multitude of good examples/areas to draw from, and was one that would show a candidate's wide experience and understanding of the global wine world. Unfortunately, this was the least well answered question on Paper 1. A number of responses simply described viticultural practices without actually doing the analyses the question requires. The question required a relatively detailed look at least two regions; some papers provided a scatter- shot of many regions' approaches, but did not address the relative value of these approaches from the question's perspective of addressing high and low value wine production. Average papers did often show an understanding of what the question was asking about, with good examples, but as one Examiner noted, "there is a lack of in-depth knowledge, facts and figures relating to the costs of viticulture and wine." In other instances, there was clear understanding, but virtually no examples to make the discussion complete, or with generic ones at best. While the question allowed for many issues to be compared and contrasted, the Examiners felt that there were between five and seven that specifically needed to be addressed. It was frustrating, as one Examiner noted, to see much written well about yield vs. quality and price, but then nothing on the implications of harvesting for high vs. low priced wines. Too many papers, sadly, were 'close' but missed because of omitting a key issue at the expense of too much discussion about some of the others. Passing papers were well organised, with clearly defined comparison of the regions and with good analyses comparing methods used by different estates and different regions. Even here, however, it was often noted that many papers failed to more closely examine the financial implications of some decisions taken. Question 2:

commentary: Referencing at least three wine regions, discuss how climate change is influencing grape growers' viticultural practices. Responses to this question may have been organised by region, or practices; only two did the former! The question required comparative analyses, not simply a litany of issues climate change is causing globally. Certainly, it was critical to include discussion of issues such as water and canopy management, disease and pest control, frost/hail pressure, legal aspects resulting from appellation 10 rules and economic pressures. This question asked for real-world solutions to the challenges across different climates/regions. Some papers only considered warm climates, without an adequate discussion of climate change in cooler ones. The question required a solid technical understanding of key viticultural practices that would need to change as the climate does. A number of papers showed an understanding and general knowledge about a specific issue, but then failed to note, for example, how important pruning/canopy management practices would need to change in compensation for climate change. This question highlighted for Examiners a significant problem seen across all of Paper 1; factual errors. Where a response shows a clear error, such as placing Katnook Estate in Barossa Valley rather than properly in Coonawarra, it will undermine credibility of the rest of the paper's discussion. Candidates need to write from authority, and given that a question such as this and many others on Paper 1 ask about generally concrete issues, factual errors are inexcusable. Question 3:

commentary: Identify the most important trunk diseases in vineyards around the world. How can they be best controlled and managed? This technically demanding question was answered relatively well, given the precise knowledge required. Critical to success here was answering both parts of this question. Less successful papers did well on identifying the most important trunk diseases, but failed to consider in depth control and management. Key to a successful answer was an acknowledgement of the global reach of these diseases: differences, varieties, treatments. A passing paper had to include at least three of the four to five key diseases noted globally. Many papers discussed Esca and Eutypa, but left out Botryosphaeria and Phomopsis. The best papers highlighted diseases affecting younger vines specifically, like Petri disease or black foot disease. A few papers got into long discussions about phylloxera and/or flavescence dorée; these are not trunk diseases! Factual errors, such as claiming that five to seven year old vines are middle-aged, or that GTD's are caused by viruses, not fungi, reflected poorly on candidates' knowledge and weakened their argument significantly. Examiners noted a strong dependence on one or two particular examples that are indicative of the same 'textbook' source, or an article. Examiners commented that many papers simply didn't do an adequate job of comparing and contrasting various techniques to deal with these diseases depending on location and climate. Positively, the best papers, as one Examiner commented: "Answers the question and answers key points. Good introduction, conclusion and structure. Includes good critical analysis with good comparative examples to support analysis, with a global range. Good writing style- A+" Question 4:

commentary: Is the use of cover crops worthwhile in viticulture? This was the most successfully answered question on this year's Paper 1. Perhaps because the question had a certain "Op-Ed" aspect, requiring a candidate to express an opinion (based upon sound factual examples and knowledge, however), this made for more fluid discussion. In a few papers, however this led to sweeping generalizations, such as "Cover crops are very necessary for viticulture". This question demanded clear understanding of what cover crops do, in different climates, and depending on availability of water. A number of papers, Examiners noted, were overly descriptive, though studded with examples. These generally answered a different question than posed, i.e. What do cover crops do? The question as set was asking for an analysis that looked at cover crops as one component of viticulture, perhaps in relation to climate change, or to the unique challenge of a particular terroir, but also considered the effectiveness of a given approach. It was not enough to list examples of where cover crops are used or not; it was necessary to discuss their utility 11 in the context of their intended purpose. Advantages and disadvantages needed to be addressed, and examples used to demonstrate where the use of cover crops may be considered 'worthwhile'. Good candidates used four to six positive or negative reasons, each discussed well. Those that did not focused narrowly on fewer ones such as soaking up excess rainfall in cooler humid areas, or not using them in more arid climates. Good papers noted more nuanced utility; for example, cover crops used to prevent erosion and help with water penetration in the harsh Douro climate. Good answers were attuned to the particular uniqueness of various sites relative to slope, site vigor and frost potential or certification for organic viticulture. It was also useful to consider the economic utility of cover crops, considering the extra cost entailed in planting/cultivating cover crops relative to the wine type and value produced. Question 5:

commentary: What is the role of pruning when managing an established vineyard? This was a question that needed a definition of pruning, relative to working in a functioning vineyard. The question was about how pruning a vine affects vineyard growth, quality and economic value and not about describing pruning techniques. A good answer had to define and explain the key purposes of pruning, but always in the context of the question. Smart answers addressed winter pruning, spring/summer pruning (hedging, sucker thinning), and where appropriate, 'green' pruning of less mature clusters to even out maturation or remove deficient fruit (under-ripe, raisined, or rotten berries). It was critical for a passing paper to address the issue of pruning relative to specific varieties and wine styles, and the timing of pruning and treatments for pruning wounds (at least in passing). Good papers addressed both the advantages and disadvantages of hand-pruning vs. mechanical, especially with regard to the economic costs and style of wine being produced. Too many non-passing papers were "more concerned with the mechanics of pruning than the role it plays", as one Examiner commented. A passing paper had to deal with the primary purpose of pruning, establishing yield, with comparison and methodology depending on wine style; e.g. short cane pruning with densely planted Pinot noir in Gevrey Chambertin vs. high-trained quadrilateral cordon with low density spacing in the Central Valley of California. It was clear to Examiners that too many answers lacked understanding of how winter pruning can strongly affect aspects of ventilation, ease of harvest, disease control or frost alleviation as well as yield. More answers addressed these issues from the perspective of summer pruning and/or simple canopy management. Again, this question saw several papers that used generic arguments or examples, without showing more concrete ones that illustrated the writer's real understanding and consideration of the question. commentary: Old vines have a mystique to them. What are the practical challenges and solutions to maintaining vineyards of old vines? The topic of this question is one which fascinates anyone interested in wine, everyone has an opinion about the superiority of old vine wine! But this question was all about the unique viticultural challenges old vines present in order to continue their existence. It was important to define old vines; Examiners saw everything from 15 to 20 years old as a minimum age, to 60 years. Considering that the average lifespan today globally for vines is in the 20 to 30 year range, a passing paper had to consider old vines in the context of the location being 12 discussed, and be clear about how this definition is often conditioned by regulations (e.g. the Barossa Charter), the historical nature of a vineyard region, or its modernity. Provided examples were given which accorded with the writer's premise, different definitions for old vines were allowed. This question required a substantial knowledge about what problems confront older vines; whether these are related to poor vigour, decrease in productivity, susceptibility to disease, especially trunk diseases or pruning wounds. Not addressing these issues and focussing mainly on the potentially higher quality from a subjective belief in old vines making the best wines, without the critical examination dictated by the question, resulted in failure. The issue of 'maintenance' had to be addressed. The economics of maintaining an old vineyard had also to be considered, particularly in light of increasing mechanization in vineyards with lower costs, vs. the expensive manual labour that old vines almost always require. Over-fertilization of old vines, in the hope of keeping them healthier, had to be weighed in relation to soil or rootstock vigour, as this can stress and overtax an old vine's system. Several papers made the mistake of saying that old vines are more susceptible to drought/water stress. As the Examiners noted repeatedly the opposite is true, as evidenced by their longevity under diverse, often harsh conditions, in places like South Africa, Australia, Santorini and elsewhere. A key challenge for maintaining old vineyards is the difficulty/inability to use more mechanization for their care. This was certainly something that a passing paper had to address; a number of papers did not do so, or only with a minor reference. Older vines require more personal, experienced care, which is difficult to mechanise, though not impossible given enough money and knowledge of a vineyard's capacity for a radical change in its make-up. Answers that focussed on fewer issues relative to the question, but did so thoroughly, generally achieved higher marks than those which tried to throw in as much as possible, without the appropriate depth of knowledge or examples to support the argument. 13

commentary: Examine the advantages and disadvantages of deliberate stem inclusion, or additions, during the winemaking process. Candidates who did well focussed on the question at hand - the advantages and disadvantages of deliberate stem inclusion across all wine styles and the whole winemaking process. Too many candidates just gave us a list of who is doing what with stems. Examples should be used to support an argument, not be the argument themselves. We expected candidates to cover the entire winemaking process, within the scope of Paper 2, not just fermentation. We also expected students to cover white, rosé and red table winemaking as well as mentioning sparkling and fortified wines. Students needed to demonstrate an understanding of why and how stems are used in the winemaking process and then discuss the advantages and disadvantages of their inclusion. Candidates are reminded to think about winemaking as a process and to consider where stem inclusion may be warranted and what the outcome of that would be - both advantageous and disadvantageous. Students tended to disregard stems within white wines with alarming regularity. Given the amount of natural wines, qvevri style wines, etc, more could have been discussed. Whilst the argument for stems was often good, the argument against the use of stems was often lacking. Given most wines are destemmed, this could have been argued better. Advantages for stems tend to be concentrated in the three varieties: Grenache, Syrah and Pinot Noir. Given comparisons were needed, varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot could have been cited as varieties that may be less appropriate for stem inclusion. Question 2:

Candidates needed to define inexpensive (using local or international currency) and off-dry. Legal limits set by the OIV should have been mentioned to support the argument. Sugar levels could be defined in terms of perception, but it was important candidates demonstrated an understanding of the legal definition of off-dry. This was another question covering the whole winemaking process. Candidates should have covered fruit ripeness, sugar concentration options in the winery, absolute need for hygiene, options for stopping fermentation, options for adding back sweetness and additions to prevent refermentation. Examples should only be used to support the argument, not be the argument 15 themselves. Sterile filtration at bottling could have been mentioned but candidates who failed to do so were not penalised. Students are reminded to be polite - inexpensive does not equal poor quality. Many students were derisive of these wine styles. This acts as a reminder to students that they need to cover ALL wine styles in their studies - not just focus on premium wine production. This was a technical paper and lack of technical understanding was displayed in many responses. We are looking for critical thinking and application of knowledge. Examiners comments reflected this. This was another popular question which was focussed on the processes and choices made during winemaking and post-fermentation maturation. The candidate needed to provide a sensible definition of the scope of winemaking - some limited consideration of the vineyard processes was allowed but the primary focus should have been on the vinification process. Ageing potential needed to be defined, finished wine needed to be defined. Examples, as always, needed to be supportive of arguments. One examiner asked: "How do some candidates think a list of examples is enough to pass?" Students should have discussed why a particular process affects the ageing potential of a wine. As always, still wine, sparkling and fortified wine should have been discussed, as well as entry level through to ultra-premium wines. Too many candidates focussed solely on the premium end of the market and neglected entry level wines. Interestingly, too many candidates only discussed red wines. There should have been plenty of scope for candidates to provide meaningful examples of what certain winemakers choose to do, why, and the impact on ageing potential. Lack of essay structure, no definition, limited scope and failure to discuss the "whys and wherefores" were the most common errors. We also urge students that, if they quote a well-known wine or region, they must spell it correctly. Question 6:

Again, the argument requires global knowledge of the supply chain and routes to market and it was felt that there was a great deal of purely superficial knowledge in this regard. This question may have been relatively straightforward for those who work in more commercial roles in the industry but a lot more difficult for those who do not. Examples tended to relate to one or two geographies, however it is important to demonstrate a broader knowledge. Equally, the examples need to be accurate - an examiner's faith in the candidate is quickly lost by inaccurate or fabricated answers. There were a few excellent answers on this question. Overall though this was not well answered due to a lack of authenticity or credibility in a lot of the writing. Question 3:

question_text: How important are environmental credentials in marketing wine?
paper_preamble: 3iv. Theory Paper Four Simon Thorpe MW Question 1:
theory_chair_report: Theory Panel Chair Report Neil Tully MW This year's theory exam produced 30 full theory passes, representing a 31.25% pass rate (2017 = 32.7%), and two single paper re-sits. These results demonstrate that a good number of candidates in this year's theory exam came into the exam room with an appropriate level of knowledge and understanding and, importantly, knew how to deploy that knowledge to good effect in response to the questions set. Many of the unsuccessful candidates, whilst perhaps having the necessary knowledge, were unable to use it effectively. Candidates would be well advised to gauge the level of depth and detail required for a successful response to a question at MW level. Many of the questions set could have been answered in a superficial manner with a basic level of detail, but the MW exam does require a certain precision and insight, of which candidates should be very conscious. In combination with an appropriate level of depth and detail, examiners are also looking for evidence of analytical thought. Very often, simply repeating processes or procedures will not suffice. Equally an overabundance of examples can sometimes mask a lack of fundamental understanding. Examiners across all theory papers this year commented on the repeated use of a limited number of examples. On theory paper 2, one examiner noted 21 out of 56 papers using the same reference to Domaine Dujac. While it is not unsurprising that material from seminars may be widely cited, it does not indicate a broad frame of reference. While the more commonly used examples may for very good reasons be seen as "go to" examples, examples taken from a candidate's own experience and enquiry, used appropriately, will stand out all the more. However, a word of caution; when using examples over-familiarity, even if those individuals being cited are well-known to the candidate, does not strike a suitable tone: "At Churton in Marlborough, Sam will decide to include stems…", and in another example: "According to Mike, the perceived benefit of inclusion of stems…". It should be emphasised that those candidates whose first language is not English, and who are not extremely comfortable writing in English, should seriously consider writing in their native language. In summary, candidates looking to elevate their marks would be well advised to consider first whether they are writing with an appropriate level of depth and detail, secondly whether they are showing evidence of critical analysis. This should all be conveyed in a suitable tone, and underpinned with appropriately chosen examples. 9 3i. Theory Paper One Joel Butler MW General Comments This year's
commentary: How important are environmental credentials in marketing wine? To quote from the examiners' indicative answer: The key point for candidates to recognise is that this is a marketing question, asking them to assess the importance of environmental credentials, not just to list them. They should examine and evaluate every aspect of a winery's environmental footprint (vineyard practices, use of energy, container used, closure used, transportation to market), and discuss to what extent this affects consumers' buying behaviour. This is not a winemaking or viticultural question, it's about marketing. It is also a question which requires an opinion, and argument - there is no right or wrong viewpoint, but it is difficult to argue against the growing consumer demand for wines with environmentally friendly credentials. 21 A clear structure needed to be provided to this question - answering from the viewpoint of the marketeer could be quite successful, but it is no good simply listing ways in which wine can exhibit environmental friendliness if that isn't then related to what the consumer feels about it. Geographical variations in demand from a market perspective was vital, especially where it was possible to give empirical evidence to support the point (such as the high and growing percentage of Scandinavian tenders which stipulate organic). There were a handful of excellent answers; those that provided clarity of thought process, good and interesting examples, relevant links between credentials and propensity to increase spend, consumer acceptance or demand for environmentally friendly wines and an understanding of how wine sits in the context of other food categories. In general, the main areas of challenge for candidates lay in not addressing the marketing nature of the question, and in delivering sweeping statements not backed up by factual evidence. Perhaps the somewhat unusual structure of the question "examine the extent to which" put candidates off, but in effect it only means "how much". The subject matter was relatively narrow, which meant that a good understanding of the key points was essential, as was the need to deploy critical thinking skill. Which examples are best? We are 22 really exploring both perceived and real scarcity - so how can this be managed? Is there a consumer benefit to scarcity? What are the downsides to scarcity? it's important to look beyond just price as a benefit to both producer and customer. Too many candidates couldn't demonstrate sufficient detailed knowledge on amounts of wine produced in the classic "icon" wines. In the opinion of the examiners, if you are short of detailed information and examples on a subject then best to avoid it. It was surprising that so many candidates (48) undertook this question and only a very small number passed. 23

question_text: Can wine be considered a social good?
paper_preamble: 3v. Theory Paper Five Beverley Blanning MW General comments The standard of essay writing improves every year and there are fewer answers which are completely out of line. The difference between a pass and a fail is less clear cut than it has been in the past. While there is a clear minimum standard for a pass, often there isn't anything specific that gets a candidate over the line. It is more a question of authoritative insight, clear communication of ideas and a balanced, convincing argument that elevate an answer to MW standard. Advice to candidates when approaching this exam: - Answer the question set, not the question you wish had been set; - Think as broadly as possible and consider the wording of the question carefully; - Avoid using the first person, singular or plural; - Avoid using headings; - Don't be afraid to challenge conventional wisdom (but always back up your arguments with facts); - Always put both sides of an argument; - Reference key facts, especially those that sound unlikely; - Spell correctly the names of people and wines in your examples. commentary: Can wine be considered a social good? We were looking for a clear definition of a social good from the outset as being something that benefits society as a whole (it might have been helpful to cite examples of social goods, such as clean air, healthcare, literacy, and so on). Many candidates stumbled at this first hurdle: either they failed to define the term, or their essays showed that they had not grasped the meaning of the question. This led to simplistic answers with the inevitable conclusion that wine is 'a good thing', which is not what we were asking. It is always advisable to consider both sides of the question, in other words, the arguments for and against. Arguments that might support the idea of wine being a social good might include: its cultural, religious and historical importance; it supports small agricultural economies; it facilitates social cohesion and well-being; it generates tax income; it has certain associations with longevity and good health. Arguments against could include: social and health problems; religious objections; legislation and taxation; costs to society. Many answers were superficial, limited in scope, one-sided and lacking in examples. There was a lot of content about responsible drinking, which is not really relevant to this question. The examiners noted that some candidates persist in giving wine special status within the alcohol sector, implying that wine drinkers are never binge drinkers nor alcoholics. Such a line of argument would require strong supporting evidence to be taken seriously. This was a question that invited examination of the many contentious issues surrounding wine. It was remarkable that, while the answer to the question would undoubtedly be a firm 'no' from many (if not most) in society, hardly any candidates considered this possibility, with 21 of the 24 answers concluding that wine was a social good. 24 Question 2:

commentary: How can the wine industry attract new consumers? This question was set in the hope of eliciting original thought and innovative ideas from the candidates. It was a straightforward and popular question, but the examiners reported few good answers and the pass rate was quite low. What happened? Perhaps the single biggest mistake was candidates' failure to distinguish between new consumers and existing consumers. Some essays were entirely based on how to increase sales among existing consumers. Others wrote solely of Millennials, ignoring every other type of potential new consumer. 'New' is not necessarily 'young'. Equally, when discussing 'the wine industry', candidates needed to break this down into producers, retailers, importers, opinion leaders, and so on. Successful answers showed understanding of current global wine consumption patterns and identified different strategies that could be adopted for different potential consumers and different markets. It must be stressed that this is not a paper 4 question, so the scope of enquiry was expected to be wider. Candidates could have looked at learnings from recent successes in attracting new consumers, or from other markets. They could have discussed the challenges of attracting new consumers, such as the complexity of the product, taste prejudices, cultural, religious, generational perceptions, presence of competing products, etc. At the same time, it is important in a question like this to present one's own ideas, and not just regurgitate what is happening right now. We expect candidates to show they have an informed point of view and innovative ideas are always welcome. 3. If

Many answers failed to do this and simply chose personal favourites. From this narrow starting point, it was an uphill struggle for them to achieve sufficient marks for a pass when so much that could have been said was missing. We were asking candidates to choose wines for humanity, not for themselves, so we were looking for a clear consideration of what was most essential to preserve for others. There were, however, some very interesting and original essays, where candidates demonstrated their passion, but also their wide knowledge of the complex world of wine. This was a wide-ranging question, with scope for the best candidates to shine. Stronger answers compared and contrasted different potential choices and were balanced in taking a broad, global view and considering the impacts for various parts of the quality/price spectrum. They gave relevant and diverse supporting examples and equal weight to each of the varieties chosen. Arguments for classic varieties were almost always stronger than those for more unusual ones, as they have proven styles, history, global plantings, consumer popularity, etc. Some candidates spent too much time on florid descriptions of wines at the expense of making a persuasive argument. 4.

This proved problematic for some, who confused elitism with inequality and even sexism. 25 If correctly defined, there were many avenues to be explored to address whether elitism is an inherent problem in wine. An historical perspective was needed, with comparison to present day attitudes. Whether or not elitism is considered an inherent problem requires candidates to examine whether this is a perceived problem somehow related to wine more than other goods, so reference to other markets would have been helpful also. Other areas that could have been addressed include: actual or perceived elitism; wine classification systems; the role of wine qualifications; sales channels and changes in the way wine is bought and sold; whether elitism is a problem, or a positive in some markets or circles; who suffers from elitism and who benefits? 5.

theory_chair_report: Theory Panel Chair Report Neil Tully MW This year's theory exam produced 30 full theory passes, representing a 31.25% pass rate (2017 = 32.7%), and two single paper re-sits. These results demonstrate that a good number of candidates in this year's theory exam came into the exam room with an appropriate level of knowledge and understanding and, importantly, knew how to deploy that knowledge to good effect in response to the questions set. Many of the unsuccessful candidates, whilst perhaps having the necessary knowledge, were unable to use it effectively. Candidates would be well advised to gauge the level of depth and detail required for a successful response to a question at MW level. Many of the questions set could have been answered in a superficial manner with a basic level of detail, but the MW exam does require a certain precision and insight, of which candidates should be very conscious. In combination with an appropriate level of depth and detail, examiners are also looking for evidence of analytical thought. Very often, simply repeating processes or procedures will not suffice. Equally an overabundance of examples can sometimes mask a lack of fundamental understanding. Examiners across all theory papers this year commented on the repeated use of a limited number of examples. On theory paper 2, one examiner noted 21 out of 56 papers using the same reference to Domaine Dujac. While it is not unsurprising that material from seminars may be widely cited, it does not indicate a broad frame of reference. While the more commonly used examples may for very good reasons be seen as "go to" examples, examples taken from a candidate's own experience and enquiry, used appropriately, will stand out all the more. However, a word of caution; when using examples over-familiarity, even if those individuals being cited are well-known to the candidate, does not strike a suitable tone: "At Churton in Marlborough, Sam will decide to include stems…", and in another example: "According to Mike, the perceived benefit of inclusion of stems…". It should be emphasised that those candidates whose first language is not English, and who are not extremely comfortable writing in English, should seriously consider writing in their native language. In summary, candidates looking to elevate their marks would be well advised to consider first whether they are writing with an appropriate level of depth and detail, secondly whether they are showing evidence of critical analysis. commentary: Do wine consumers need wine experts? This was another popular question. Sadly, it was poorly answered by most candidates. The question needed a really clear and broad definition of 'experts', including media commentators, auctioneers, MWs, buyers, retailers, winemakers, consultants, educators etc, and understanding of the varying and different types of wine expertise. A large number of candidates restricted their definition to journalists and therefore gave very incomplete answers. Most also missed the opportunity to talk about the importance of experts involved in the production of wine, which was a significant omission. Also important was to distinguish between different types of wine consumer, as there will be different requirements of expertise for different types of consumer (generational, geographical, socio-economic, education level, etc). As always, we were looking for a global perspective, and for candidates to demonstrate an understanding of the dynamic nature of how and why consumers might need wine experts. An appreciation of the changing perception of experts and the rise in importance of peer reviews was also an area to explore.

question_text: Are yield restrictions necessary to produce high-quality wine?
paper_preamble: Theory Exam Paper One - Joel Butler MW General Comments The Paper 1 examiners were pleased to see a slight uplift in the overall standard of responses to this year's paper; although Question 2 was the least well-answered question, the examiners saw many well thought through answers to the question set. While the examiners welcome appropriate use of examples, these should be specific and used to demonstrate a point being made in response to the question, rather than being used as "generic" examples that do little to serve the candidate's purpose in answering the question. These tend to indicate an overly "bookish" learning, rather than real world understanding. Definition of terms needs to be carefully judged. While precision is important, it is not necessary to slavishly define every term in each question. The examiners urge candidates to check that facts being used are accurate. Information is available from many sources, and all may not necessarily be reliable. The examiners noted a number of inaccurate "facts" from possibly questionable sources. Q1.
theory_chair_report: Theory Chair Report - Neil Tully MW This year's theory exam produced 33 passes, representing a 32% pass rate (2018 = 31.25%). This continues the trend of the last few years which indicates that many candidates are well prepared across all five theory papers. A good number of candidates this year passed the theory exam with high marks across all papers; really excellent papers written with authority, clarity and conviction. Importantly, marks across all five theory papers were generally consistent at all levels. This is in contrast to previous years where the examiners often saw quite uneven performance in the theory exam with, for example strong marks on Papers 1, 2 and 3, and much lower marks on Papers 4 and 5, or conversely, great Papers 4 and 5 and much less successful "technical" papers 1, 2 and 3. This suggests that candidates are better prepared across the whole exam, and this is to be commended. However, there were a significant number of candidates with marks some way below the pass mark, this was often on account of not only a general lack of appropriate knowledge but also a failure to address the questions being asked. This is a matter raised by examiners on all theory papers. Candidates are reminded to first read the question very carefully. Much thought and consideration is put into the wording of our questions, candidates should be under no illusion as to what is being asked. Very often the reason for candidates not achieving better marks is that the question answered was not the same as the question being asked. Candidates must be honest with themselves; do not write an answer to the question you want to see, but write an answer to the question that is on the page in front of you. Do not be willfully blind about this. The examiners know exactly what they are looking for, and obfuscation will not work. Questions will sometimes ask for critical analysis. This is also an aspect that is often avoided or overlooked. This element is often at the heart of the question, it is the analysis that will demonstrate "mastery" to the examiners, therefore candidates who do not address this element of any question will seriously limit their potential marks. The theory examiners on all papers are looking for evidence of applied knowledge. Candidates approaching the exam with English not as their first language are advised to consider very carefully the best option of whether to have papers translated or to write in English. 3 b)
commentary: Are yield restrictions necessary to produce high-quality wine? A successful response to this question required finding meaningful connections between various methods of yield restriction and their impact on wine quality and by doing so arriving at a conclusive answer. A more "opinion-editorial" approach would have been unlikely to pass. Generally, the question was well answered; most candidates managed to grasp the essential understanding that it was about vineyards where yield manipulation was consciously required. Correctly, they did not spend much time writing about low yielding vineyards based upon old vines, restrictive soils, etc. Poor time management was an issue for a number of candidates, evidenced by a paucity of writing, shortage of examples, or leaving out discussion of a key issue such as canopy management. The examiners in particular were looking to see where candidates, in evaluating "are" (yield restrictions necessary) were able to demonstrate "how" (they might be necessary to produce high- quality wine) in order to answer the question successfully. The best answers also noted clearly that with new viticultural techniques, new clones, better understanding of vine balance and the effect of climate change in certain locales, low yields are not as necessary to producing high-quality wines as they once were. More importantly, there is no 'one size fits all' for lowering yields to produce high-quality grapes.

commentary: Q2. Your company has acquired a vineyard which has been producing grapes for bulk wine. How would you convert the vineyard to high-quality wine production? 4 This question was approached from a number of different angles by candidates, some choosing to focus on a single, notional vineyard and others writing in more general terms. Both could have been successful as long as they considered the main principles and importantly focused on conversion. Many answers rolled out good information on how to set up and farm a vineyard for high quality, but didn't necessarily address the real-world issues of converting a vineyard from one purpose to another. A number of responses that discussed step by step how to establish a vineyard missed the point of the question, which is about converting. Many answers missed chances to show mastery and real- world understanding by too quickly assuming that replanting was the only way to go. It was important to consider the viticulture issues of conversion: changing the canopy (management), manipulating water availability/delivery, altering vine density, pruning, row alignment etc. Examiners found too many papers where the argument presented for conversion used examples not related to a real bulk wine vineyard type. One paper noted that Chambolle-Musigny producer (hardly bulk wine area) Frederick Mugnier said that "while spur pruning can be used successfully on young vines, it is better in time to convert them to cane-pruning to restrict the yields and achieve more terroir-driven wines." A similar notation from an overachieving grower in the Midi would have been more accurate and justifiable.

commentary: Q3. How can drought tolerance be achieved in viticulture? This was not a question about climate change. Candidates were expected to evaluate the viticultural techniques available to achieve drought tolerance of vines. It was relevant to consider how learnings from regions that have long operated in near-drought conditions, such as Napa, Mendoza and parts of Australia, may be applied in vineyards experiencing changing climatic conditions, or indeed in new regions that have hitherto been considered unsuitable for viticulture due to existing drought conditions. Being Theory Paper 1, the emphasis should be on viticulture. Under consideration would be recent research and technologies such as infra-red aerial photography, as well as important viticultural issues such as adaptive rootstocks, cultivar change, cover crop and canopy management, improved irrigation regimes and changing appellation restrictions in non-permitted irrigation areas, not forgetting the issue of actual water availability in areas where irrigation is permitted. Passing papers provided solid discussion and examples from around the globe for at least five to six of these viticultural issues, presented in a balanced manner. The best papers interlinked various tactics, reflecting the fact that no one single aspect could be solely responsible for managing drought tolerance. Less successful responses omitted one or more critical issues such as canopy management, soil analyses/amendments, or cover crops, and dwelt strongly on water management or selecting drought-tolerant scions. Very few papers discussed using new hybrids or crosses. The very small 5 percentage of papers that discussed the important research being done at viticultural research centers on the subject indicated a significant knowledge gap. Q4. Mildews

commentary: continue to blight vineyards. What strategies might a vineyard manager implement to reduce the risk? This was a question that could only be answered well if one had a good knowledge of the standard remedies. Examiners were primarily looking for an informed discussion about what are considered the two most important mildews: downy mildew and powdery mildew. Botrytis and Phomopsis could have been included in the discussion, as long as the two primary mildews were more strongly considered. The best papers noted that there are many fungicides and treatments available and that they must be rotated, or not all used together, in order to ensure that the mildews don't develop resistance. It was important to consider not just copper and sulphur treatments, but also to acknowledge and explain how alternative, resistant varieties, canopy management, vineyard hygiene, climate modelling/forecasting, and the critical timing of treatments can reduce mildew damage. While no one was expected in this paper to be intimate with the exact formulas, candidates should have considered the differences between contact, local systemic and fully systemic treatments; few addressed the different modes of action that lie behind a diverse, sustainable approach to preventing mildew. The Examiners were looking for a wide-ranging discussion of different strategies, including organic/biodynamic approaches, in particular noting that there is no easy organic/biodynamic substitute for using copper sulphate, which is why it is accepted (although now in the EU at much reduced rates). commentary: are the most critical considerations for selecting rootstock when establishing a new vineyard? This question was the best answered on the paper. As with Question 4, it required specific discussion and clear examples that demonstrated the writer's knowledge of rootstock traits, limitations and consequences for their use. Examiners were looking for papers that properly addressed matters including: 1. A primary consideration for rootstocks is protection from pests in the soil such as phylloxera and nematodes. 2. Rootstocks are used to address specific challenges or limitations of a site, such as soil chemistry, or excess/inadequate water, or soil structure/fertility. 3. The compatibility and health status of the scion. 4. How vine vigour can be impacted; therefore requiring consideration of variety, spacing, vine size, soil nutrients, salinity. 6 5. How rootstock choices can affect yield, ripening time, quality and flavour which, in turn, strongly influence the end goal of wine quality. 6. How the relationship between all of these must be taken into consideration: there is no simple, single answer to choosing a rootstock. Good papers had specific examples that supported their discussion, rather than simply enumerating facts about rootstocks without context. Many papers, for example, noted that nematode presence was a critical consideration for selecting a rootstock, offering some examples. But then didn't analyse why, and for what kind of nematode and potential disease impact they may vector, and under what circumstances. Good papers also delineated interconnected reasons for using a rootstock; for example to deal with nematodes and drought tolerance. Several papers also considered how climate change may require new rootstock use in traditional areas where changing circumstances such as drought conditions require a new approach. On the other hand, a number of non-passing papers provided few to no examples of rootstocks needed for particular issues. Or, if the main reasons for using rootstocks were listed, there was often a lack of analysis addressing the question: the key considerations when planting a new vineyard.

question_text: How can a winemaker manage the impact of oxygen during the winemaking process?
paper_preamble: Theory Exam Paper Two - Meg Brodtmann MW General Comments Examiners made a number of comments that apply to all questions on this year's Theory Paper 2. Examples should be used to support a statement rather than as the statement itself. commentary: How can a winemaker manage the impact of oxygen during the winemaking process? In many cases, candidates did not have the depth of knowledge that was required to answer this question successfully, whilst those that did shone brightly with a number of excellent scripts. Structure in this question was crucial as there was a great opportunity to waffle about oxygen in so many forms. The best answers really focused on the question and were very competent. The challenge was to get to grips with how winemakers can manage oxygen, responses that failed to confront this stood out quickly. There were too many formulaic answers with a simple regurgitation of facts rather than providing an actual answer to the question as set. Many candidates concentrated on what oxygen does rather than discussing how a winemaker can manage the impact of oxygen. Too many candidates did not answer the actual question, preferring to write about how Prosecco and Champagne are made without referring to the question of quality and at which steps quality could be influenced throughout the entire production process. Where Sekt was mentioned, most candidates took for granted that Sekt is always made from Riesling which demonstrated a lack of awareness of today's premium Sekt production with Burgundian varieties. Quality in sparkling wine production does not just come from ageing on lees; every part of the winemaking process can impact on the final quality of the wine and candidates should have covered this. As a result, very few considered the fact that any given method is not a guarantee of quality - it is the process within those methods that determines the outcomes. 10 d)

question_text: Explain which pre-bottling treatments and QC analyses you would consider most important for an inexpensive, organic, vegan wine.
paper_preamble: Theory Exam Paper Three - Caroline Gilby MW General Comments Many of the questions on this year's Theory Paper 3 required thought and analysis rather than simply trotting out a pre-prepared essay. As ever, strong candidates demonstrated appropriate technical knowledge, supported by real world evidence and examples. However, too many lacked factual knowledge or the ability to adapt their answers. One examiner commented that a number of candidates appeared to reproduce pre-prepared essays vaguely relevant to the question, without focussing sufficiently on the perspective of the question. Such a strategy is unlikely to be successful, as any such answer is likely to include much that is irrelevant and to omit much that is relevant. Another complaint was that some candidates limited the focus and ground to be discussed in their introduction, but without justification. Examiners also commented that too often examples were not well used; they tended to be 'dropped in' briefly rather than incorporated into a critical discussion. There was also a number of otherwise good candidates who limited their examples to the Southern Hemisphere rather than showing evidence of global wine knowledge. It bears repeating that Paper 3 is a technical paper and it is expected that candidates will have a firm grasp of some key factual and numerical information. EU limits for SO2 use and units, being clear about whether the numbers refer to total or free SO2; typical levels of free SO2 for various styles; actual values for pH; permitted and actual usage levels for common wine additives; pore sizes for filtration - this is all key knowledge for MWs. It is worth double-checking these too - numbers like 100 g/l SO2 or 45 micron filters cropped up. Vague comments like "lower levels of SO2" are not sufficient - actual numbers are required. Inaccurate use of "sulphur" instead of sulphites or sulphur dioxide still crops up regularly, and while this may be widespread shorthand among winemakers, there are important differences between sulphur as an element and its compounds. Another bugbear is candidates who believe that "brett" is bacterial - Brettanomyces is a yeast species and yeast are a completely different kingdom of life to bacteria. Similarly, TCA is not a bacterial problem and VA is not a microbial problem in itself but may be the result of microbial metabolism. Unfortunately, errors like these undermine confidence in the candidate. Technical knowledge and topics such as QA/QC may not be the most glamorous part of the wine industry, but they are critical in ensuring wine reaches the consumer in sound condition. In general candidates who did not pass wrote superficial answers that were descriptive rather than analytical, lacked examples and numbers. There were also a few frustrating candidates who wrote well but didn't answer the question so could not score good marks. 11 Q1.

commentary: Explain which pre-bottling treatments and QC analyses you would consider most important for an inexpensive, organic, vegan wine. Key understanding: • Need for pre-bottling treatments and QC analyses in general; risks if not undertaken - practical risks in terms of impact on wine, and commercial and legal/regulatory risks. • Market positioning and category (inexpensive, vegan, organic); factors affecting choices of treatments, taking account of relevant regulation and cost of treatments. • Awareness of production pressures of inexpensive wine - likely to be high volume, quicker winery throughput (no time for barrels, natural clarification etc). • Awareness of legislation for organic wine - must comply with EU or other applicable rules which specifies permitted additives and processing techniques (e.g. no electrodialysis, reverse osmosis etc). Lower sulphite levels than non-organic wine. • Understanding of implications for vegan claim - no animal products even as processing aids. This question required candidates to think about implications of the specified parameters. Most candidates did understand that the question was meant to cover one wine with all these parameters, but some considered three different wines. An inexpensive wine should have been defined. Markets do vary, but a 20 Euro wine is hardly inexpensive for most. It was not helpful to use examples of premium wines such as classed growth Bordeaux or Ridge to illustrate this answer. It was also reasonable to expect that an inexpensive wine needed to be stable, clear, free from hazes and deposits and possibly would contain residual sugar, and would likely need to be prepared quickly and in large volumes. Many answers were let down by lack of awareness of permitted additives and treatments under organic regulations - so proposing electrodialysis, CMC, sorbic acid, PVPP or Velcorin were errors. question_text: What steps should a winemaker take, in preparation for bottling and at bottling, to prevent microbial spoilage? Consider both red and white wines.
paper_preamble: Theory Exam Paper Three - Caroline Gilby MW General Comments Many of the questions on this year's Theory Paper 3 required thought and analysis rather than simply trotting out a pre-prepared essay. As ever, strong candidates demonstrated appropriate technical knowledge, supported by real world evidence and examples. However, too many lacked factual knowledge or the ability to adapt their answers. One examiner commented that a number of candidates appeared to reproduce pre-prepared essays vaguely relevant to the question, without focussing sufficiently on the perspective of the question. Such a strategy is unlikely to be successful, as any such answer is likely to include much that is irrelevant and to omit much that is relevant. Another complaint was that some candidates limited the focus and ground to be discussed in their introduction, but without justification. Examiners also commented that too often examples were not well used; they tended to be 'dropped in' briefly rather than incorporated into a critical discussion. There was also a number of otherwise good candidates who limited their examples to the Southern Hemisphere rather than showing evidence of global wine knowledge. It bears repeating that Paper 3 is a technical paper and it is expected that candidates will have a firm grasp of some key factual and numerical information. EU limits for SO2 use and units, being clear about whether the numbers refer to total or free SO2; typical levels of free SO2 for various styles; actual values for pH; permitted and actual usage levels for common wine additives; pore sizes for filtration - this is all key knowledge for MWs. It is worth double-checking these too - numbers like 100 g/l SO2 or 45 micron filters cropped up. Vague comments like "lower levels of SO2" are not sufficient - actual numbers are required. Inaccurate use of "sulphur" instead of sulphites or sulphur dioxide still crops up regularly, and while this may be widespread shorthand among winemakers, there are important differences between sulphur as an element and its compounds. Another bugbear is candidates who believe that "brett" is bacterial - Brettanomyces is a yeast species and yeast are a completely different kingdom of life to bacteria. Similarly, TCA is not a bacterial problem and VA is not a microbial problem in itself but may be the result of microbial metabolism. Unfortunately, errors like these undermine confidence in the candidate. Technical knowledge and topics such as QA/QC may not be the most glamorous part of the wine industry, but they are critical in ensuring wine reaches the consumer in sound condition. In general candidates who did not pass wrote superficial answers that were descriptive rather than analytical, lacked examples and numbers. There were also a few frustrating candidates who wrote well but didn't answer the question so could not score good marks. 11 Q1.
theory_chair_report: Theory Chair Report - Neil Tully MW This year's theory exam produced 33 passes, representing a 32% pass rate (2018 = 31.25%). This continues the trend of the last few years which indicates that many candidates are well prepared across all five theory papers. A good number of candidates this year passed the theory exam with high marks across all papers; really excellent papers written with authority, clarity and conviction. Importantly, marks across all five theory papers were generally consistent at all levels. This is in contrast to previous years where the examiners often saw quite uneven performance in the theory exam with, for example strong marks on Papers 1, 2 and 3, and much lower marks on Papers 4 and 5, or conversely, great Papers 4 and 5 and much less successful "technical" papers 1, 2 and 3. This suggests that candidates are better prepared across the whole exam, and this is to be commended. However, there were a significant number of candidates with marks some way below the pass mark, this was often on account of not only a general lack of appropriate knowledge but also a failure to address the questions being asked. This is a matter raised by examiners on all theory papers. Candidates are reminded to first read the question very carefully. Much thought and consideration is put into the wording of our questions, candidates should be under no illusion as to what is being asked. Very often the reason for candidates not achieving better marks is that the question answered was not the same as the question being asked.
