commentary: Great wine is made in the vineyard.' Do you agree? This was the paper's most popular question, and the examiners felt that candidates should have been very well prepared to answer such a straightforward question. A clear definition of "great wine" at the outset was vital. On the whole, the phrase was quite well defined and addressed; but a significant number of candidates offered very nebulous definitions (or often just implied one) and these answers then lost focus and failed to clearly answer the question. Strong definitions of great wine were precise (not just BLIC-based), but also acknowledged that there are diverse, subtle differences of perspectives on membership of this category, from different producers, businesses and consumers. Only the best answers really delved into what separated great wines from the merely very good. Some candidates set the bar far too low, considering in too much detail the sanitary condition of the grapes, as if that is what really distinguishes great wines from their peers. At a crude level, the relative importance of natural versus human inputs, in the vineyard and winery, was generally understood. However, it was surprising how many answers failed to appreciate the central importance of 'terroir', as a key aspect to be discussed. Many answers failed to unpick the contribution to greatness of specific vineyards and plots ('terroir'), from the management practices in those vineyards, which made their arguments muddled. Many candidates also thought listing wines made from respected terroirs was somehow sufficient. The answer needed to show how terroir and viticulture influenced grapes, in a way that raises quality and imbues the resulting wine with special character. Vineyard and winery process are not really equivalent in terms of the nature or granularity of their respective contribution to a wine's character, but were mostly treated very simplistically as two sides of the same coin. Disappointingly, the crucial, broader socio-cultural and economic contributions to the perceived greatness of wine - such as history, reputation and critical acclaim, classifications, supply and demand, control of distribution, marketing, and so on - were rarely explored. Overall, the examiners felt that the level of clear and original analysis was very disappointing for paper 5. Better answers offered a nuanced reframing of the question, arguing that great wine "is born/begins in the vineyard", and contrasted wines whose character is typically attributed to terroir (such as burgundy) with those that owe much of their character to process (for example, sparkling or fortifieds), using telling examples. Stronger answers often also observed that even the latter tend to prize superior vineyard sites, adding another dimension to their arguments. The sophisticated minority broadened the question beyond "vineyard vs. winery" arguments, to argue that a central component of greatness is market perception, and hence that there is a post-production contribution from critics, collectors, marketeers and so on. 2.

question_text: Could it be argued that recent climate change has been a good thing for wine lovers?
paper_preamble: Paper five report 2024: Paper chair, Ken MacKay MW General Comments In general, the examiners felt that many candidates were less prepared for this paper than in previous years. An overall impression of a lower standard in answers was perhaps reflected in the lower pass rate for the paper. However, it is also important to point out that this was compounded by a significant number of incomplete papers, where only one question or, in some cases, no questions at all were attempted. For all of these candidates, it was obviously either impossible or exceptionally challenging to be able to pass the paper. Paper 5 is about mastery of communication in wine, and requires accurate, clear, balanced and critical answers, supported by relevant examples, displaying good insight into the global world of wine. Unfortunately, the examiners reported that the standard of written English was quite poor this year. Only the minority of essays could be described as well written, let alone excellent, in this regard. Some of the commonest failings are worth highlighting. Overall, arguments were often poorly structured and rambling, containing irrelevant examples, facts or arguments, or not focused on answering the specific question. The examiners would like to emphasise that candidates must resist the urge to crowbar 'interesting facts' into their answers. If something is not directly relevant to answering a specific question, it almost certainly weakens the answer if it's included, no matter how dazzling and impressive the information might seem to be. Furthermore, many papers were answered at a very high level, in broad, simplistic terms, with little in the way of supporting detail or clear, specific examples or evidence. At the same time, candidates frequently took an overly narrow focus in their answers to questions and failed to cover enough of the breadth of different considerations, such as financial impacts, or different global or supply chain perspectives. Finally, a large number or papers (perhaps the highest in recent years) contained multiple misspelled wine/winery/winemaker names and technical wine terms. This is clearly not something which reflects mastery of wine. Many of these fundamental essentials have been emphasised in previous examiners' reports, which we would direct any candidates who have an aspiration to pass the exam to review and digest, as they are an enormously helpful source of guidance. 1. '
theory_chair_report: Theory Exam Chair Report, Beverley Blanning MW The examiners have noted that this year's report covers much of the same ground as in previous years, so much of what follows may sound rather familiar. Nevertheless, candidates are advised to study this and earlier examiners' reports in order to understand the same areas of weakness that repeatedly lead to a fail result in the theory examination, regardless of the questions set. Recurring themes include a failure to answer the question asked and a lack of the critical analysis needed to provide an MW-level answer. As in previous years, we observed many students who seem unable to use examples to support the points they are making. Very often, we see instead a simple reporting (and sometimes blind acceptance) of what somebody has told them, rather than analysis or application of this information to the question at hand. We also see the same examples repeated across questions and papers, which suggests insufficient experience and depth of preparation for this part of the MW exam. The theory exam requires candidates to have both breadth and depth of knowledge, and to be able to apply this learning to specific questions, under time pressure, to show clear understanding of the global world of wine. Do not underestimate the challenge. We are looking for candidates to demonstrate mastery, which means you need to show a) that you understand the material you are writing about; b) that you realise there are usually several ways of looking at a question; and c) that you can weigh up the pros and cons of an issue and come to your own, informed conclusions. All of this goes beyond merely describing what winemaker X says or does. Before writing, ask yourself: How is this relevant? Does this answer the question? Have I considered all aspects of this question? Resist the temptation to insert your favourite examples where they are not relevant. Remember that examples will frequently be enhanced by comparisons to alternative points of view from other sources. The examiners have commented on a general decline in the standard of answers this year across all papers, which is reflected in a lower overall pass rate compared to last year of 21%. There did appear to be a higher than usual number of particularly ill-prepared candidates this year, with some answering the wrong number of questions across multiple papers, or failing to turn up to one or more papers, resulting in some very low marks. Although we had fewer candidates failing all papers this year, a surprising number scored marks low enough to lose a future attempt at the examination. As well as studying the reports of the paper chairs that follow, prospective candidates are advised to be clear on the content of the syllabus for each paper and to practice writing essays to time. As seen in previous years, some candidates appear to arrive in the exam room with pre-prepared essays in their heads which they struggled to adapt to the specific questions with which they were faced. A preferable revision tactic might be to research and learn an area of the syllabus and then practice answering essay questions unseen, under exam conditions. Finally, on a more positive note there were, as always, some excellent candidates who ably demonstrated the mastery required to achieve a pass. The theory examination is a challenge, but with the right approach and preparation it is quite possible to succeed.
commentary: Could it be argued that recent climate change has been a good thing for wine lovers? A definition of "recent climate change" was an obvious requirement to answer this essay, along with a clarification from the candidate as to whom they understood "wine lovers" to be. The essay demanded specific knowledge of at least some of the evidence, in terms of statistics and facts, to support recent climate change concerns. The question required candidates to understand that this was not just an essay on viticultural impacts of climate change, but an analysis into whether it had benefited areas across the entire supply chain, and the impact of climate change on winemaking processes, styles, quality, packaging, logistics and consumer choice. Some insight into financial consequences, and the knock-on effects for consumer pricing, were also a critical part of this essay. Overall, it was essential that answers offered a clear, logical and balanced argument, considering the positive impacts of climate change for wine lovers and also its negative consequences. This was in many ways a good, old fashioned 'pros and cons' answer, which required interesting global examples to support the argument, as well as a strong, clear conclusion. Poorer answers often did not outline in enough depth what "recent climate change" looked like, many referring to global warming and its impact on vineyards rather than considering a broader perspective, essential for paper 5, of its impact on prices, packaging, style, etc. "Wine lovers" were often not defined at all, when it was necessary to understand to whom the candidate understood this term referred. The main issue for non-passing answers, however, was the lack of a balanced argument. Many answers focused either purely, or mostly, on arguing how recent climate change could be seen to be a good thing, whereas the only way to answer 'could it be argued' was to give equal time to the opposing view. Poorer answers also did not include enough specific facts or examples to pass and ended with weak conclusions, often not answering the question. Good answers defined key terms from the outset and discussed the topic in a logical way, taking different impacts of climate change and considering their pros and cons across the supply chain, and the multi-dimensional impact of climate change on aspects of grape growing, winemaking, wine style, packaging, logistics and price. Specific, relevant and global examples also lifted these essays, along with more critical thought around the subject. The best answers evidenced superb recall of relevant climate change statistics and factors in well written, thoughtful, clearly structured, balanced essays with relevant, focused and global examples, as well as some consideration of different consumer segments (wine lovers) and impacts on the entire wine production chain. 3.

commentary: Propose and justify a contemporary definition of 'fine wine' and discuss how perspectives on this may have changed over time. Obviously, there was no simple 'correct' answer to this question. The term 'fine wine' is used frequently in wine circles, but it is a complex, evolving and necessarily fluid category, which has been interpreted somewhat differently, depending on historical moment and national/individual perspectives. Historically, the term was arguably used more consistently and was certainly less inclusive for most, with membership consisting predominantly of French wines and perhaps other specific famous European regions. To answer this question clearly, it was essential that the candidate proposed a contemporary definition, rather than simply list various opinions of what elements might contribute to making a wine "fine". Whatever route was chosen for the argument, this seemingly simple question required some basic knowledge of the fine wine trade and its history, and the ability to stake out the boundaries of a definition that could explain why wine X would be called "fine" and wine Y not. Very few answers managed to demonstrate either quality. Naïve or outdated perspectives and shaky logic often rubbed shoulders with some extraordinary factual errors. Such a broad topic offers an almost limitless choice of examples, so why some candidates opted for producers or events with which they were clearly unfamiliar was mystifying. One recurring misconception saw candidates cite Millennials' indifference to fine wine. Sotheby's claim 30% of their wine and spirits clientele in 2022 was under 40, and fine wine is attracting similar interest to other luxury categories (watches, cars, etc.) among young Americans with high disposable income. The overall decline in alcohol consumption among younger age brackets does not necessarily map onto waning interest at the top end - quite possibly the reverse. Many answers focused too much on narrow considerations. These included the importance of packaging, which, although it is typically aligned with a wine's status, does not itself make the wine fine. Others focused almost entirely on sustainability and organics, which are also not, in themselves, justifications of "fine wine", although many fine wines are also sustainably produced. A few also presented simplistic arguments regarding 'natural' wine status or price, in isolation, which were also unconvincing. Very few essays focused on the distinction between fine wine and high-quality wine, and whether this line had become blurred. Passing answers reflected an understanding that "fine wine" developed to differentiate the best wines and justify a wine's value or price to buyers, consumers or collectors. Crucially, they also presented a clear definition, supported by evidence. The handful of good answers addressed more of the semantic and practical points invited by the question. Why (and to whom) is the term useful at all? To what extent does "fine wine" overlap with good wine? Who gets to say whether a wine is fine or not? How have these considerations changed, if at all? These better answers considered diverse 'perspectives' (for example, of collectors, retailers, auctioneers, restaurant owners, sommeliers, writers/critics, different international markets) and multiple change-drivers, such as the shifting influences of classifications, influencers (of all kinds), long-term investment potential, age-worthiness, routes to market, and historical reputation (of both producer and region), as well as perceived rarity. Relevant parallels with the art market, members' clubs, the evolution of 'fine dining', or socioeconomic categories, were also helpful supporting insights. 4.

commentary: How and why should governments influence wine consumption? Three key words should have been underlined before attempting this question. "How" and "why" are the most obvious and answers needed to balance both considerations, using global examples. However, it was also essential that the answer addressed what governments "should" do, to influence wine consumption. Governments can and do exert a substantial influence over how, where, when - and at what price - wine can be consumed. A review of some of the main tools of influence a government has was essential. These include: taxes, import quotas, export subsidies and financial support, public campaigns, minimum pricing, age restriction, labelling requirements, advertising restrictions, as well as complex licensing and permit schemes. Linked to this was the necessary consideration of the many motivations governments have to influence consumption, which include: reducing the harmful effects of alcohol on both individual and public health and safety; consumer protection through clear and standardised labelling and packaging regulations; supporting the local wine industry on domestic and export markets; protection of minors and vulnerable groups; preserving culturally important traditions and tourism; and regulating commerce. A common mistake was to address only half of the question - both the "how" or "why" needed to be answered, but many answers focused on one or the other. Poorer answers also lacked appropriate realism and balance, by offering somewhat blinkered criticism of the WHO's position on 'safe' doses of alcohol and naively questioning the compelling scientific evidence for the negative consequences of alcohol consumption. Similarly, poorer answers lacked appropriate insight into different global markets and failed to consider the many different types of regulations/policies that governments could implement. Weaker answers were mostly entirely descriptive, rather than evaluative, mentioning something such as the Loi Évin, for instance, but then failing to elaborate whether it was a sensible approach or whether other countries should adopt similar restrictions. The 'should' part of the question required a clear opinion and many candidates failed to provide any answers. Passing answers avoided these pitfalls and managed to answer all elements of the question, as well as weigh the government's responsibility to protect the health and welfare of its citizens (with specific mention of things like cancer, liver disease, alcoholism and mental health problems) against their, potentially conflicting, responsibility of promoting responsible wine consumption, to support the wine industry's important cultural and economic contributions to society. Specific global examples, such as comparative tax rates, were important to support the 'how' part of the evidence. Better passes engaged with the question as to whether wine should be a 'special case' amongst alcohol products, due to its particular balance of positive and negative socio-economic impacts. The best answers wove in a truly global, critical and balanced view - with diverse, relevant examples from around the world - which reflected an understanding of how and why governments influence wine consumption, and clearly justified opinions on when it should, or should not, interfere. 5.

commentary: How important is the concept of a defined wine region? This was a popular question, with many successful answers, but also a large number of poorer answers. In answering this question, candidates needed to be clear in their definition of a "defined wine region", before clearly weighing up the importance of this concept in a logical, well-evidenced discussion. Crucially, candidates needed to grasp that this question was not an abstract one and, therefore, it required a systematic consideration of to whom the concept of a defined wine region might be important, across all parts of the global wine supply chain. Many poorer answers failed to give any clear definition of the scope of "defined wine regions", which hampered their ability to clearly delve into their importance, in all their various forms. Weaker answers also failed to present their argument in any logical structure or show any balanced, critical thinking around the topic, often being very 'top line' or 'stream of consciousness' in style. Many of these answers used very generic examples, only referring to entire regions throughout the whole essay rather than focusing in on more specific and valuable illustrations of their points. The majority of candidates failed to reference Champagne or the CIVC which felt like a major omission, given its importance and dominance of its category, supported by strong protectionism. Overall, there was a disappointing level of understanding in many answers about the importance and value of wine regions to producers - based on terroir and other factors, and how these elements define, support and protect them - and many candidates simply addressed the topic from a consumer marketing perspective. Passing answers were able to demonstrate a clear, well-structured argument, and provided more precise examples (whether producer, retailer, wholesaler etc.), that lifted their answers. The best answers examined the question with some historical context, considering the reasons for defining wine regions and how their relevance might have evolved. They also explored the issue in greater depth, for example: referencing retail outlets that merchandise their wines by style, rather than region; exploring brands and varietals, and the importance of other cues on wine labels, to different demographics, markets and producers; considering cross-regional blends; or even drawing useful illustrative comparisons with other consumer products, to highlight some of the particular differences of the wine category.

question_text: How effectively can vineyard pests and diseases be controlled without using agrochemicals?
paper_preamble: Paper One Report: Paper Chair , Rhys Pender MW General c omments It is a familiar theme over recent years that many of the same issues tend to hold back the success rate in p aper one . There were some positives though. One positive this year was that there was a lot of impressive knowledge demonstrated on the p aper one syllabus. However, this knowledge too often comes across more as book learning and lacks analysis and insight from the candidate. What will give success in an MW paper is a candidate who can pull together all their textbook knowledge, link it with real - li fe practical situations, see the bigger picture and then come down with their own point of view taking all those things into account, supporting these opinions with global examples. Often candidates just list the textbook stuff and throw in a couple of examples of what people are doing, missing the crucial analysis. Another positive this year is that there were a lot of great and diverse examples, not just what was gleaned at seminars. While this is great to see, an issue for some candidates seems to be the urge to focus too much on examples. Many students seem concer ned with packing in (often interesting) examples without remembering to link each of these back to contributing to answering the question. This means their essays read more like a list of what people are doing rather than showing the expected level of anal ysis and consideration of the question. A couple of general points to consider with laying out an essay. Many students are writing a good introduction, outlining what they plan to cover, setting the scene, promising a great paper. Yet often, the main body of the essay fails to address what was p romised in the introduction, resulting in the question being poorly answered. Questions nearly always have a couple of parts to them. Part of it will need theory knowledge, part will need linking to specific details. Good practice will see every paragraph showing knowledge, linking it to practical realities, backing it with examples and showing individual analysis and opinion. 1)
theory_chair_report: Theory Chair: Beverley Blanning MW The main observation from the 2025 t heory e xam is that results are improving and candidates are achieving better grades. Of the 96 candidates sitting this year's theory exam there were 27 passes, a pass rate of 28.1% compared to 19.8% in 2024. It may be cold comfort to those who are reading this re port having failed t heory, but the overall standard of papers in 2025 showed a marked improvement on that of recent years. Candidates passing one or more papers are to be commended for achieving MW standard in at least part of the exam. Only two years ago, two - thirds of candidates sitting the Theory exam failed all papers; that figure is now below 40 per cent. There was a higher pass rate overall compared to last year, but also a higher percentage of non - passing candidates scoring well on one or more papers. More candidates are passing more papers - and even if these results are insufficient to result in an over all pass, it is hopefully just a matter of time and experience before they do. The key question, therefore, is how to convert a pass on a couple of papers to a successful result overall? This is where the examiners' report is so useful. While it delves into the detail of each question on the exam, it also highlights recurring general themes that provide the clues to why papers pass or fail. These examiners insights are invaluable tools, especially for candidates who are unsure of why their essays are not achieving a passing grade. Some of the more salient points cited by the examiners are the following: • The theory papers require candidates to show critical analysis, yet many essays remain descriptive and lacking the analysis required to achieve a passing grade: " Many answers that do not meet required standards are purely descriptive and fail to apply knowledge in the context of the question. " • The examiners point to evidence of rote learning at the expense of understanding. • Examples must, in all cases, be relevant. One paper chair comments that often, " candidates fail to understand the purpose of examples. " • Check facts and examples for accuracy. • Candidates are encouraged to critically evaluate source materials, rather than accepting producer claims at face value. • Any conclusions must be supported by evidence and critical reasoning. This applies not just to the final paragraph of an essay, but each point made throughout. It is not enough simply to report what others have said. • It is difficult to achieve a passing grade if parts of a question are not answered. • Candidates are encouraged to challenge assumptions, to show depth as well as breadth, and to 'think beyond the headlines'. I wish future exam candidates every success in their studies and trust that the information contained in this report will serve as a useful guide to achieving a pass in the t heory exam. 3
commentary: How effectively can vineyard pests and diseases be controlled without using agrochemicals? This was by far the more popular of the section A questions, chosen by over 90% of candidates. There were mixed results. A lot of answers to this question were overly descriptive, just giving a list of examples of what people are doing without showing the necessary analysis. Many students seemed to read the question as "how can pests and diseases be controlled without using agrochemicals", missing the word "effectively". The word "effectively" signalled a requirement for analysis, weighing up the complex re al - life difficulties and practical challenges for grape growers looking to control pests and diseases without using agrochemicals. A lot of papers listed many examples, but showing an understanding of the challenges and limitations for effective use of the se controls in viticulture compared with using agrochemicals was often weak. While it was acceptable to include thoughts on protection from animal pests, some candidates allocated a disproportionate amount of emphasis here, taking away from the key areas where growers have typically relied on agrochemicals. Other candidates had the ir focus drift off to a more philosophical discussion on organic/biodynamic viticulture, its costs, quality of grapes and wines, etc. without focusing on specific pest and disease controls. There also seemed to be some misunderstanding around agrochemicals that are allowed in organic viticulture such as Bordeaux mixture. These were often referred to as a non - agrochemical option. The strongest papers focused on the practical challenges of foregoing agrochemicals while showing a solid understanding of pests and diseases and concluding how effective each control option was. 4 2) '

question_text: "Bacterial and phytoplasma diseases are the greatest threats to vine health today." Discuss.
paper_preamble: Paper One Report: Paper Chair , Rhys Pender MW General c omments It is a familiar theme over recent years that many of the same issues tend to hold back the success rate in p aper one . There were some positives though. One positive this year was that there was a lot of impressive knowledge demonstrated on the p aper one syllabus. However, this knowledge too often comes across more as book learning and lacks analysis and insight from the candidate. What will give success in an MW paper is a candidate who can pull together all their textbook knowledge, link it with real - li fe practical situations, see the bigger picture and then come down with their own point of view taking all those things into account, supporting these opinions with global examples. Often candidates just list the textbook stuff and throw in a couple of examples of what people are doing, missing the crucial analysis. Another positive this year is that there were a lot of great and diverse examples, not just what was gleaned at seminars. While this is great to see, an issue for some candidates seems to be the urge to focus too much on examples. Many students seem concer ned with packing in (often interesting) examples without remembering to link each of these back to contributing to answering the question. This means their essays read more like a list of what people are doing rather than showing the expected level of anal ysis and consideration of the question. A couple of general points to consider with laying out an essay. Many students are writing a good introduction, outlining what they plan to cover, setting the scene, promising a great paper. Yet often, the main body of the essay fails to address what was p romised in the introduction, resulting in the question being poorly answered. Questions nearly always have a couple of parts to them. Part of it will need theory knowledge, part will need linking to specific details. Good practice will see every paragraph showing knowledge, linking it to practical realities, backing it with examples and showing individual analysis and opinion. 1)

commentary: 3) How can artificial intelligence be used in viticulture to improve the quality of wine grapes? There was a relatively good pass rate in this question, although the answers were quite mixed. The less successful candidates spent a lot of time looking at how AI was used in other industries or just being overly big picture without offering specific links to grape growing and grape quality. Many failed even to define grape quality in the first place. The best candidates showed some creative and interesting ways that AI is - and can be - used, linking back to specific wine quality parameters they had defined as important measures of grape quality. The key areas of using data to get accurate and speedy information to growers to allow them to make more precise vineyard decisions and improve sustainability, was well answered in many essays. 4)

commentary: To what extent does soil management affect the quality of wine grapes? This was a straightforward question that allowed students to show their theory knowledge while also affording the opportunity for some critical thinking, by linking the knowledge back to wine grape quality. Unfortunately, many candidates took the opportuni ty to show considerable knowledge about options for soil management but failed to answer the second part of the question linking to quality. Defining and linking to quality of wine grapes had to be specific, getting down to details on how different management techniques might affect sugars, acid, tannin, flavour concentration, balance, complexity, yield, etc. Many students simply referred to "b etter quality" without any detail. The best papers showed knowledge of different soil management options, looked at "to what extent" they had an effect and linked to specific, pre - defined elements of grape quality. The most concise answers also addressed how there is no recipe and considere d different scenarios where differing management techniques were best suited. As is often the case, candidates tended to focus on small, high - quality producers without addressing large volume producer's issues, an important consideration to make for a more thorough paper. 4)

commentary: How do changing rainfall and wind patterns affect viticulture? The non - intentional trap some candidates stumbled into here, was to just see a general climate change question, and as a result wrote a generic essay that did not address in detail the specific aspects of changing rainfall and wind patterns. The weaker ones were quite descriptive without linking back to how the changing patterns affect viticulture. Examples were lacking in many cases with not enough of a global pers pective. The better papers were able to give examples of how rainfall and wind patterns were changing, seeing both negative and potentially beneficial sides and supporting their analysis with the many possible global examples from recent years. Timing of events, se verity, and addressing impacts from flowering through to harvest as well as trellis and equipment concerns proved the most thorough answers. 5)

commentary: To what extent can rootstocks be used to mitigate the effects of climate change? There is quite a lot to unpack in this question. First, candidates had to look at defining the effects of climate change and then make specific connection with different rootstocks across these different scenarios, identifying how they can help to mitigate the often - unpredictable changes. 5 Weaker papers often just focused on a descriptive list of rootstocks, their characteristics and sometimes a few examples of what certain producers are using, but without looking at how they could mitigate the effects of climate change. Others had an overly limited view of climate change effects as just hotter and drier, ignoring aspects such as frost, flood, changing pest and disease pressures, etc. It was also important to consider the "to what extent" practicalities of changing a rootstock, the cost of no fruit while the vine establishes and the gamble on guessing what the vineyard conditions will be like over the next 30 years. The better papers had excellent examples from different scenarios, considered things like whether you need a rootstock at all and looked at many practical implications. 6

question_text: Critically assess the key techniques a winemaker can use to enhance complexity and texture in bottle-fermented sparkling wines.
paper_preamble: Paper Two Report: Paper Chair, Richard Kershaw MW General c omments While candidates generally displayed sound technical knowledge, many responses remained superficial, resembling diploma - level accounts rather than the critical analysis expected at Master of Wine level. Notable strengths emerged among candidates who appeared to have practical winemaking experience and performed exceptionally well in problem - solving scenarios. Question four achieved a high pass rate, despite limited attempts, while q uestion one on bottle - fermented sparkling wine received many pass - level and several excellent responses, demonstrating both technical accuracy and a broad understanding. Successful scripts consistently defined key terms at the outset, planned essays systematically, a nd used dive rse international examples to support arguments. However, many candidates offered descriptive accounts rather than critical evaluation, producing "laundry lists" of techniques without explaining mechanisms, or weighing trade - offs, or applying knowledge in context. Some candidates appeared to be relying o n memorisation instead of genuine understanding. Confusions between pH and acidity, or bacteria and yeasts, further weakened technical credibility, with superficial statements such as "MLF softens acidity" left unexplained. Poor essay technique compounded these issues - weak time management led to verbose passages at the expense of concise analysis, while careless errors suggested rushed completion. More disciplined planning, focused writing, and attention to accuracy are essential to demonstrate the analytic al depth expected at MW level. Use of examples was also problematic. Candidates often over - relied on local or obscure producers that failed to illustrate arguments effectively, while omitting benchmark international cases that would have strengthened authority. Name - dropping without exp lanation added little value. Future success in p aper two will depend on integrating knowledge with critical thinking. Candidates must move beyond "how" to address "why," demonstrating understanding of both processes and their contextual applications. Preparation should focus on evaluation, mechanism explanation , and disciplined essay planning.

commentary: 1 ) Critically assess the key techniques a winemaker can use to enhance complexity and texture in bottle - fermented sparkling wines. This question challenged candidates to demonstrate a thorough understanding of how winemakers intentionally create complexity and texture in bottle - fermented sparkling wines, requiring an evaluation of chemical, microbiological, and physical mechanisms thr oughout the production process. The strongest scripts followed clear chronological structures, beginning with base wine considerations, including grape variety and harvest decisions, pressing regimes that distinguished between cuvée and taille fractions, and must handling techniques such as débourbage. These candidates effectively discussed fermentation choices, particularly vessel type and yeast selection, examining how these elements impact flavour layering and mouthfeel. They treated malolactic conversion as a stylistic tool rather than simply stating it as fact, consistently emphasising the importance of blending and reserve wines as methods to create depth and consistency across different cuvées. When discussing second f ermentation, better candidates evaluated the effects of tirage composition, yeast selection, and fermentation temperature on mousse quality and autolysis, effectively connecting extended lees ageing with the release of mannoproteins, lipids, and amino acid s on texture and aromatic development. Dosage was evaluated with nuance, recognising its role not only in balancing acidity but also in adding aromatic complexity through liqueur composition and integration time. 7 Most surprisingly, numerous candidates failed to mention mousse at all - specifically how fine bubbles soften perceived acidity, create creamy mid - palate weight, and support length and persistence. This represents a fundamental oversight in understanding the textural qualities of bottle - fermented wines. Several candidates overlooked crucial stages, such as base wine production, and focused disproportionately on oak influence, reserve wines, or dosage. The regional scope proved limited in many responses, with answers relying too heavily on Champagne exampl es, missing opportunities to demonstrate a global perspective through references to Cava, Franciacorta, or traditional method wines from the New World. Overall, candidates who excelled were those who moved beyond description to demonstrate a genuine understanding of how specific techniques enhance the sensory attributes in question. Success required not only knowledge of production methods but also the ab ility to critically evaluate their purpose and effect. 2 )

commentary: Evaluate the different winemaking techniques that can enhance a wine's potential for extended bottle ageing. This question required candidates to critically examine how specific winemaking and maturation decisions influence a wine's long - term stability and capacity to evolve positively in bottle. Strong answers needed to demonstrate understanding of how key interventions affect structural balance: phenolic extraction and management providing oxidative buffering in reds; protective handling or controlled oxidation strategies in whites; the critical role of low pH (typically ≤3.4) for microbial stability, colour retention and SO₂ efficacy; oxygen management through vessel choice and maturation regimes; and the strategic use of techniques like lees ageing, clarification, and blending. Candidates were expected to illustrate these principles across diverse wine styles - from reductive, high - acid whites to oxidatively handled fortified wines, traditional method sparkling wines with extended lees ageing, and sweet wines where residual sugar a nd acidity balance support longevity. The question required technical explanations of mechanisms, not merely a listing of practices. With a higher - than - average pass rate, this effectively differentiated between those candidates with genuine technical understanding and those attempting to list memorised information without critical evaluation. Phenolic management was generally well - understood, particularly for red wines, with candidates discussing extraction through cold soak, extended maceration, and cap management. For whites, both protective handling and controlled hyper - oxidation approaches were addressed effectively. The best answers explored oxygen strategies, the benefits of lees ageing, the impacts of vessel selection, and strategic blending decisions using benchmark examples. However, acidity and pH control were surprisingly poorly covered. Many candidates failed to connect low pH with improved microbial stability, colour retention, and SO₂ efficacy. Classic high - acid, long - lived styles like German Riesling, Loire Chenin Blanc or Hunter Semillon were seldom mentioned. Coverage of wine styles proved uneven, with many restricting themselves to red and white wines, ignoring sparkling, sweet, or fortified categories. This narrow focus severely limited their ability to demonstrate a comprehensive understanding across different wine types. Technical depth was often lacking, with essays providing lists without explaining the underlying mechanisms - stating, for example, that "MLF can increase ageability" without explaining how. Hygiene and microbial stability received minimal attention despite their fundamental importance. Examples frequently came from fringe regions rather than established benchmarks, while references to supplementary techniques, such as antioxidants, chelating agents, or closure implications, were rare. 8 Overall, while the best essays were analytical, technically detailed, and stylistically informed, weaker responses were descriptive, unstructured, and narrow in scope. Success required not just knowledge of practices but understanding of their mechanisms a nd the ability to evaluate their application across diverse wine styles. 3 )

commentary: Examine the roles of bacteria in winemaking. How can bacteria be managed to achieve desired outcomes? This question tested candidates' technical and practical understanding of bacteria's diverse roles in winemaking. A solid answer needed to demonstrate knowledge of beneficial bacteria - particularly Oenococcus oeni's role in malolactic fermentation - and spoil age organisms, including Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Acetobacter, and Gluconobacter. Candidates were expected to explain specific metabolic pathways: how O. oeni converts malic to lactic acid, affecting pH and wine stability; how Lactobacillus and Pediococcus produce biogenic amines and off - flavours; and how acetic acid bacteria create vol atile acidity and ethyl acetate under aerobic conditions. Management strategies should have included precise parameters - pH ranges of 3.2 - 3.5 for MLF, molecular SO₂ below 0.5 mg/L, temperatures of 18 - 22 ° C - alongside practical approaches like inoculation timi ng, oxygen exclusion and hygiene protocols. The question demanded evaluation of how bacterial management varies with wine style, from encouraging MLF in most reds to suppression in aromatic whites, with consideration of trade - offs between predictability an d terroir expression. The most alarming issue was confusion between Brettanomyces (a type of yeast) and bacteria. While most recognised O. oeni superficially, optimal conditions were poorly understood. Vague assertions such as: "MLF reduces acidity", appeared without explaining conversion chemistry. Understanding spoilage bacteria proved weakest - volatile acidity, biogenic amines, mouse taint or ropiness were listed without explanation with most candidates limiting discussion to clean fruit and cellar hygiene whilst critical deta ils - oxygen exclusion through inert gas blanketing, topped barrels, molecular SO₂ maintenance based on pH, and recognition that these aerobic organisms thrive with oxygen exposure and pH above 3.5 - were largely absent. In fact, the concept that pH below 3.2 inhibits bacteria while above 3.5 increases spoilage was rarely clear. Critical oxygen exclusion details were absent. Advanced techniques, such as lysozyme or alternative bacteria like Lactobacillus plantarum, or DMDC, were notably missing. The few candidates showing mastery covered the topic's breadth with accurate parameters while demonstrating practical understanding through relevant examples - full MLF in Syrah, partial MLF in Chablis, suppression in Riesling, higher VA acceptance in Port. They explained metabolic pathways, outlined comprehensive management strategies, and critically assessed trade - offs. 4 )

commentary: Evaluate prevention and correction strategies for each of the following issues: a) 0.9g/L volatile acidity in a Chablis wine (pH 3.2, 12.5% ABV) intended for lees ageing; b) S trong reductive aromas post - malolactic fermentation in a premium Barossa Shiraz (pH 3.8, 15% ABV) destined for 24 - month oak ageing; c) 80mg/L total sulphur dioxide in a Bordeaux blend (pH 3.6, 13.5% ABV) pre - bottling. This three - part question assessed candidates' ability to critically evaluate both preventative and corrective winemaking strategies for distinct compositional and sensory faults. While initially appearing highly technical, the question proved to be more st raightforward than expected, with specific guidance provided for the required solutions. Only eight candidates attempted it, achieving a 50% pass rate. For the Chablis scenario, the stronger candidates explained why 0.9 g/L volatile acidity was problematic, as it exceeded the 0.7 g/L sensory threshold, thereby compromising Chablis's stylistic requirements for freshness and precision. They recognised that while legal limits often exceed 0.9 g/L, this level was inappropriate for the style, noting the protective pH of 3.2, though acknowledging lees ageing risks exacerbating VA development without microbial stability. 9 Successful prevention strategies included using clean fruit to limit microbial loading, strict sanitation with oxygen exclusion, maintaining yeast health through adequate nutrients and temperature control, and implementing appropriate SO₂ regimes at 25 - 30 mg/L free SO₂ for a pH of 3.2. Correction proposals included blending with low - VA Chablis, reverse osmosis despite flavour loss risks, curtailing lees ageing if instability persisted, and sterile filtration for active spoilage organisms. However, some cand idates showed muddled reasoning, discussing producers without VA issues when asked to address high VA, suggesting reliance on memorised examples rather than applied technical knowledge. For Shiraz, better answers linked high pH to reduced SO₂ efficacy, reductive aromas to oxygen limitation and that at elevated alcohol (15%), microbial stability may still be compromised, all of which can become persistent if not addressed before extended oak ageing. Strong prevention strategies included ensuring adequate YAN, using low - H₂ S yeast strains, employing pump - overs or open - top fermenters for aeration, discontinuing vineyard sulphur sprays pre - harvest, and prompt post - MLF SO₂ addition. Correction approaches included aerative racking to volatilise H₂ S, copper fining with appropriate trials while noting thiol risks, selecting permeable barrels for oxygen exposure, and potential blending. Many candidates missed the Barossa context clue about open - top fermenters f or reducing reduction. Weaker scripts confused reduction with oxidation, offered vague solutions, or failed to recognise the importance of early intervention before oak ageing entrenches faults. The Bordeaux scenario was least well answered, revealing gaps in understanding regulatory frameworks and SO₂ correction strategies. Strong candidates identified that 180 mg/L exceeded the EU red wine limits (150 mg/L), making it unsaleable in that market. Recognising that at pH 3.6, molecular SO₂ is less active, it reduces protection, while high totals limit further additions and suppress fruit expression. Better prevention strategies included accurate molecular SO₂ - based dosing, avoiding redundant applications through monitoring, reducing microbial pressure via hygiene and oxygen exclusion, early acidification for improved SO₂ efficacy, and regular free/total SO₂ tracking. Corrections included blending with low - SO₂ components, hydrogen peroxide where permitted with precise dosing, extended maturation for natural dissipation, or marketing in countries with higher thresholds. 5 )

commentary: Considering a diversity of wine styles, critically evaluate the importance of blending to achieve consistency. This question assessed candidates' understanding of blending as both a technical and strategic tool in winemaking. Answers needed to define blending as the combination of wine components in creating a target profile and stylistic consistency as the reproduction of sensory, structural, and quality attributes across bottlings or vintages. The critical requirement was eva luating blending's importance to consistency, not merely listing practices. Candidates were expected to demonstrate how blending operates at multiple stages - from pre - fermentation, co - fermentation through to pre - bottling adjustments - across at least three wine styles. For sparkling wines, this meant explaining how reserve wines main tain the non - vintage house style; for fortified wines, how solera systems ensure absolute consistency; for still wines, how varietal or vessel blending achieves balance; and for sweet wines, how blending different harvest passes or botrytis levels creates harmony. The question demanded critical evaluation of trade - offs, recognising that blending is often more acute in high - volume commercial wines than premium single - vineyard examples, and assessing when consistency might compromise terroir expression. This was the most poorly answered question on the paper. Many candidates drifted into descriptive accounts without critically evaluating the importance of blending to consistency. The failure to define key terms suggested inadequate planning, leaving essays unfocused and rambling. Most candidates specified which wine styles they would discuss, typically covering sparkling, still, and fortified wines, but coverage proved uneven. Some omitted sparkling or fortified wines - the categories where blending most obviously ensures consistency. Many overlooked the solera system, arguably the most important blending mechanism for 10 consistency, while blending's role in managing vintage variation in climatically variable regions like Champagne or Bordeaux was underexplored. Examples were sometimes superficial, with statements like "Moët uses 100+ base wines" appearing without explaining why this matters for maintaining consistency across vintages or how reserve wines function as a stylistic anchor. Mateus rosé was cited exten sively without substantive discussion of the commercial requirements for rosé production. Only the best candidates discussed practical aspects, such as blending wines from different vessels, using blending trials to correct imbalances in acidity or alcohol , or the logistics of maintaining reserve wine stocks. These candidates understood how blending supports specific stylistic goals, evaluating when it's essential versus optional and recognising the commercial imperatives driving consistency in large - scale production. The lack of critical analysis was particularly disappointing. Most essays remained descriptive, failing to distinguish between blending as a corrective tool versus a proactive stylistic choice. Candidates didn't evaluate how blending balances commercial ob jectives against quality aspirations or assess the pressure between consistency and vintage expression. Success required moving beyond memorised examples to demonstrate genuine understanding of blending's strategic importance - not just what winemakers do, b ut why these practices matter for achieving consistency and how they contribute to commercial viability while maintaining quality. 6 )

commentary: Assess how pH influences winemaking decisions at key stages from grape to finished wine. This question tested candidates' ability to apply detailed chemical knowledge of pH across the winemaking process. Strong answers needed to define pH as the logarithmic measure of hydrogen ion concentration, cite typical ranges (2.9 - 3.1 for sparkling, 3.1 - 3.4 for whites, 3.3 - 3.8 for reds), and systematically evaluate how pH drives decisions at each stage. Candidates were expected to explain pH's influence on: microbial and oxidative stability during juice handling; yeast health and competing organisms during fermentation; MLF facilitation or suppression; SO₂ efficacy during maturation; and pre - bottling adjustments including filtration requirements. The question required specific parameters - not vague references to "high" or "low" pH - with examples illustrating how pH considerations vary across different wine styles. A large number of candidates, with varying degrees of success, answered this question. It revealed a clear divide between those with genuine technical understanding, as evidenced by their comprehensive coverage of key stages, and those who offered only sup erficial generalisations. Strong candidates systematically covered key stages, explaining how pH affects decisions from whole bunch pressing and early acidification during juice handling through to final SO₂ calculations pre - bottling. They demonstrated how a lower pH supports clean fermentation by suppressing competing microbes, while a higher pH reduces SO₂ efficacy and complicates microbial management. During MLF, they recognised that higher pH encourages LAB activity but reduces stability, with MLF itself raising pH further - dis cussing both encouragement strategies through inoculation and suppression through SO₂ or lysozyme. The best answers addressed maturation issues with spoilage organisms at elevated pH levels and recognised pre - bottling as the final opportunity for pH - informed adjustments. Significant omissions weakened many responses. Very few candidates considered the influence of pH on fining efficacy or stability management. Colour stability received minimal attention despite pH's critical role in anthocyanin stability. While cold stabil isation was covered by half the candidates, protein and tartrate stability relationships with pH were frequently overlooked. Some candidates addressed only pH adjustment methods, missing the broader question of how pH influences decisions throughout winema king. Others wasted time explaining differences between total acidity and pH rather than addressing key winemaking stages. 11 Technical depth varied dramatically. Weaker answers relied on statements like "pH affects microbial stability" without explaining the mechanism - that lower pH increases the proportion of molecular SO₂ , the antimicrobial form. A surprising number focused solely on regional examples, presumably from their home markets, suggesting a limited global perspective that is insufficient at MW level. The question effectively differentiated candidates who understood pH as a fundamental driver of winemaking decisions from those reciting memorised facts without comprehension. Success required explaining not just what happens at different pH levels but how this knowledge actively informs choices throughout the winemaking process. 12

commentary: a producer of a dry white wine that may age in bottle for up to five years, you are considering changing from natural cork stoppers to an alternative closure. What technical factors should you consider? There was a solid pass rate on this question indicating that closures are well understood. Candidates needed to understand that the closure must provide an effective seal - for at least 5 years, in this case - and could have taken the view that an inert closure to reduce change was preferred, or a clo sure that allowed some bottle development. The question did not require answers to cover marketing or end user preferences. Technical considerations include: suitability of closure to avoid taints or detrimental changes and avoid leaks; handling and fitting; effective life span; and implications for handling of the wine itself, including managing headspace. Examiners reported a good number of high - quality scripts. Where candidates did not do well, they were let down by poor understanding of technical details such as OTR (correct units showing amount/per volume/per unit of time must be given, or numbers are m eaningless) and failed to cover the larger picture of wine handling and headspace management. Descriptive answers without real analysis were also disappointing. And examples needed to be more than X does Y and give enough detail that the context is clear. 13 2)

commentary: Write concise notes on three of the following: a) Mousiness b) Light strike in bottled wine c) Elevated volatile acidity in bottled wine d) Management of a tank of rosé with free sulphur dioxide well above its ideal level. This question required candidates to have a strong understanding of 3 of the 4 topics. It was also specific that the answer needed to be concise. Therefore, if the candidate had strong knowledge on 3 of the topics, then the paper itself was not that diffic ult. Those lacking in knowledge were shown up very quickly and often candidates tended to write around the subject rather than answer the question asked. The topics mousiness and light - strike were probably the two best answered questions, although a number of candidates were not aware of implications of riboflavin levels and sulphur - containing amino acids. The answer on volatile acidity was probably the most varied - some excellent answers but weak answers failed to address 'in a bottled wine'. If they wrot e on VA in general, they missed the key aspect of the QC investigation to establish how VA arose in bottled wine and could usefully have referred to how to prevent its future occurrence. Therefore , reading the question and answering accordingly was key her e rather than just writing about volatile acidity. The question of managing high FSO2 in a rosé was probably the weakest in terms of answers, showing that many candidates just do not have a strong grasp of winemaking practices outside of the standard proce sses implemented by winemakers. Those that provided relevant examples to support their explanations scored well, often helping those into a pass versus those that fell short. 3 )

commentary: What are the key factors to consider when deciding whether to cold stabilise white and red wines? What quality control measures are required to test that wine is stable? This question had the lowest pass mark on this paper. Several candidates interpreted the second part of this question as covering quality control measures generally addressing wine stability, not just measures for testing for cold stability, as was expecte d in setting the question. This was allowed for. However, candidates who did not address the second part of the question did lose marks. Candidates should be aware that cold stabilisation is an important winemaking process that helps prevent unwanted cryst allisation in wine, particularly tartrate crystals, when the wine is stored at low temperatures. It is not simply about chill filtering the wine. However, winemakers must carefully consider various factors when deciding whether or not to cold stabilise a w ine, as it involves trade - offs between quality, cost, and desired characteristics. Many candidates did not explain why tartrate stabilisation is less important for red than for white or rosé wine. Weaker answers were descriptive about methods for cold stabilising often with strong emphasis on chill filtering, rather than providing sufficient analysis about why it might be done and the trade - offs and implications for wine quality of the methods avail able. A lot of answers did not address the second part of the question about tests for tartrate stability, and this was important to cover for good marks. Better answers looked at wine chemistry rather than just focusing on practical or economic factors, b ut several who did attempt to do this were unable to explain it properly. It looks as though candidates had been told something by a producer but struggled to justify it in their essays. Overall, the first part of the question (factors to consider in decid ing whether to cold stabilise) was answered much better than the second (QC measures relevant to tartrate stability), but many candidates appeared not to have real breadth or depth of understanding on either aspect. With some notable exceptions, candidates continue to misunderstand the purpose of examples and thus how to use them in their answers: for example, a bald statement that '[Supermarket X] requires [Winery Y] to cold stabilise its wines' is of limited value as an example - it needs to cover why ( e .g. transport in cold temperatures, likely customer responses etc). 14 4) Why

commentary: are fining agents used in winemaking? For each of the following wines, explain which factors might influence the choice of fining agent used: a) entry - level South African Chenin Blanc b) DOCG Barolo, and c) vegan AOC Côtes de Provence rosé. This was, in general, a better answered question than the one on cold stability. The question was broken into two parts and both required addressing, which a number of candidates failed to do. Answers needed to be clear that the purposes of fining are clar ification and stabilisation, and that it may also be used to modify colour and adjust astringency/ tannin levels. It is also important to be aware that it is speedier than a natural settling process, so saves money for producer and ultimately, consumer, an d may have logistical benefits. Most candidates had a reasonable grasp of the issues relating to fining, with two common exceptions: (i) cost of the fining agent chosen and cost implications of the time fining would take with each option; and (ii) labelling/allergen considerations - thou gh not essential to cover, it would have been useful to show awareness. Many candidates were unable to use relevant producer examples to discuss critically alternative fining practices, suggesting that they need to travel/speak to visiting winemakers more than they have done to date. A number of candidates also wasted time addressing pre - fermentation fining choices, whereas they should be aware that p aper three addresses only the post - fermentation stage of winemaking unless otherwise stated. Where many came unstuck was their basic winemaking knowledge of factors influencing the choice of fining agent and which fining agent is most applicable to the wine style in question. Those that could do this, scored well. The answer to the DOCG Barolo was the best answered part of the question, perhaps because it is a more traditional wine style with which everyone is familiar. Those that provided relevant examples to support their explanation scored well. Most candidates supported their answer with exampl es but often the examples were not well thought through and showed little association with the points they should have been supporting. 15

paper_preamble: Paper Four Report: Paper Chair, James Davis MW General c omments Overall, it was pleasing to see an improvement in the pass rate from 2024 to 2025. However, it was clear that many essays were borderline rather than compelling passes. For paper four , writing style and language are especially important as candidates are encouraged to foster a fact - based argument that can be drawn from knowledge of different markets for wine around the world. Examiners noted weak English, slangy intros, or odd phrasing in some instances. Similarly, candidates should make sure their essays h ave relevance and focus. Often essays were surface - level, lacking critical thinking or industry insight. I would encourage students to directly address the question set with a clear argument and language. Try to avoid slang and ensure that any acronyms you use are explained, and globally relevant rather than country - specific, as they are otherwise unlikely to be understood. Ensure you have data points and examples to back up your narrative. We are not seeking perfection, but we are looking for sufficient ev idence of mastery to warrant a passing grade. 1)

commentary: How has Champagne maintained its primacy in the world of sparkling wine? Overall, it was answered quite poorly. Those essays that succeeded covered the important r ole of the CIVC in organising the industry along with the importance of branding allied to Champagne's luxury positioning. commentary: To what extent can government wine monopolies benefit producers, retailers and consumers? This was a reasonably well - answered, if unpopular, question. Pass - level essays showed solid knowledge of key issues, including pricing mechanisms, sustainability and public health, the tender process, monopoly dynamics and distribution and logistics. It w as good to see some essays refer to the role of quality assurance that a monopoly structure can indirectly (or directly) offer a producer. Those essays that were strongest focused critical analysis on the producer and retailer implications of monopoly and the question of consumer choice and quality, along with the balance between restriction and efficiency. Weaker essays tended to focus on one side of the argument with more superficial analysis or insufficient depth, for example, the variation in monopoly s tructures across jurisdictions. Often, there was an over - reliance on Canada and Scandinavia as example markets, and the examiners noted that US control states were frequently omitted or underexplored. The best essays were well structured, nuanced, and grou nded in definition and evidence, addressing, for example, the debate over whether monopolies help or hinder small/niche producers. 5)

commentary: Wineries are increasingly selling direct to consumers. Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of this approach compared to other routes to market. This was the most popular essay on the paper and there were many good answers. Examiners noted that strong essays demonstrated a solid understanding of the benefits of direct to consumer (DTC), including control over the customer experience, higher margins , brand building, and the role of data capture (loyalty schemes such as Wine Clubs). These benefits were then assessed in the context of market structure, consumer trends, and the strategic implications of DTC models. Strong essays showed frequent use of r eal - world examples, showing awareness of different producer scales and geographic markets, including, for example, references to the nascent English wine industry and the associated development of DTC. The best responses acknowledged the complexity of hybr id Routes to Market ( RTM ) s and recognised that DTC is not a one - size - fits - all model, discussing DTC in the context of a broader, multi - channel strategy. However, many essays lacked adequate discussion of alternative RTMs, such as traditional wholesale and e - commerce partnerships. Also lacking in many essays was consideration of the high costs of running DTC and the upfront capital investment often required. Generally, there was a heavy US and Canada bias, with Europe and other global markets underrepresented. Examiners also noted t hat there was little comparative analysis of how DTC plays out in rural compared to urban locations. The best essays defined DTC clearly and placed it within the wider RTM context, treating DTC as one of several options, not an isolated strategy. 6)

commentary: Discuss the evolution of the négociant business format in Burgundy over the last 15 years, explaining the contributing factors. Are current conditions financially sustainable? This question, which required specific knowledge of the Burgundy market, was not at all popular, but those who attempted it answered reasonably well. Some candidates demonstrated confusion about the role and scope of négociants, often misrepresenting them as merely brokers, or confusing them with wine domaines, and sometimes incorrectly stating that négociants began as recently as the 1980s. Some candidates only referred to new négociants, not thinking of historically successful examples such as Drouhin or Bichot. Examples used were sometimes inappropriate, such as using Domaine cases in what is a négociant - focused question. Several essays were incomplete or very brief, limiting depth of analysis. While introductions were generally strong, with good paramet er setting and relevant examples, candidates often showed gaps in knowledge, for example believing all growers make their own wine or that négociants are declining in number. Stronger candidates included thoughtful writing, clear structure, and attention t o recent financial aspects. Overall, greater focus on the full scope of the 17 négociant business, with more detailed technical and historical accuracy, would have enhanced the quality of responses. 18

question_text: What will be the likely impact on the global wine industry if health warnings about cancer risks become increasingly mandatory on wine labels? Discuss the implications of such changes for producers, marketers and consumers.
paper_preamble: Paper Five Report: Paper Chair, Ken MacKay MW General c omments Many candidates seemed better prepared for this year's paper five , compared to last year. There was a relatively balanced spread of answers across the five questions, although question two was the runaway favourite. As always, the strongest candidates were those who combined clear structure, directness in answering the question, a global perspective, relevant and varied examples, and critical analysis. Across all questions, weaker essays tended to be overly descriptive, lack good examples, or focused on just one aspect of the question rather than answering all parts evenly. Question one , in particular, showed that even well - prepared candidates can struggle if they don't allocate time or analysis evenly to all parts of the question. Many candidates also failed to define key terms at the outset, which led to a lack of focus and confusing, unconvincing arguments which didn't link well to their conclusions. A nother recurring weakness was a narrow geographical lens, with examples clustered in the UK, USA and EU; candidates are reminded that p aper five always requires a global view and appropriate diversity of examples. Often, answers revealed a tendency to overstate certain solutions (notably No/Lo wines in Q2) without bothering to interrogate their limitations or feasibility. Common technical missteps included misquoting or misrepresenting sources (for example, Dr Laura Catena's views on health and wine), simple factual inaccuracies in product details (such as the alcohol content of Moscato d'Asti) or producer name spellings, and confusion between related but distinct concepts (for instance, conflating complex moderation - oriented drinking trends with permanent abstention). Opportunities for deeper critical engagement - such as exploring trade - offs, unintended consequences, or tensions between goals (e.g. sustainability versus cost, technology innovation versus displaced l abour) - were frequently missed. commentary: the question. 1 ) What will be the likely impact on the global wine industry if health warnings about cancer risks become increasingly mandatory on wine labels? Discuss the implications for producers, marketers and consumers. This is a 'hot topic' and it was clear that many candidates had researched it well in advance of the exam. However, many answers - even those with good, general background knowledge - failed to fully address all parts of the question, or were too descripti ve and simplistic about the issue. Often, candidates spent too much time outlining the background with unnecessary detail before getting around to delivering substantive discussion on the implications for producers, marketers and consumers. Dr Laura Catena 's position on this issue was very frequently misrepresented. Consumers were rarely treated with any global or demographic resolution. Another common weakness was the lack of supporting evidence and examples - or examples concentrated solely on the UK, USA or EU. A global perspective is essential to a high - quality p aper five response, and candidates must ensure they reflect the global nature of the industry. Many other weaker answers had an overly narrow focus entirely on label changes and costs, rather tha n on wider implications such as the impact on sales and global over - supply, the potential opportunity for premiumisation, or the pressure to reduce alcohol levels. A further shortcoming in many scripts was a lack of engagement with the wider commercial and regulatory context. Few candidates explored how mandatory health warnings could affect market positioning, brand equity, consumer trust, or long - term category grow th, beyond the immediate packaging implications. Opportunities to discuss potential shifts in consumer perception, changes in on - and off - trade behaviour, and the possible reallocation of marketing spend were often missed. Similarly, there was limited disc ussion of how producers in different market segments - from bulk exporters to fine wine estates - might face very different challenges and opportunities. 19 Pass - level candidates avoided most of these pitfalls and applied their knowledge evenly across the three areas mentioned in the question, supported by global examples. Stronger candidates considered the issue in greater depth and breadth, presenting more b alanced arguments, better supported by more diverse examples from different regions, and engaged with current health discourse in a nuanced way. They also considered potential benefits to all three groups - demonstrating an ability to think holistically an d critically about the situation. 2 )

More candidates are passing more papers - and even if these results are insufficient to result in an over all pass, it is hopefully just a matter of time and experience before they do. The key question, therefore, is how to convert a pass on a couple of papers to a successful result overall? This is where the examiners' report is so useful. While it delves into the detail of each question on the exam, it also highlights recurring general themes that provide the clues to why papers pass or fail. " • Check facts and examples for accuracy. • Candidates are encouraged to critically evaluate source materials, rather than accepting producer claims at face value. • Any conclusions must be supported by evidence and critical reasoning. commentary: How is the global wine industry adapting to changing societal attitudes towards alcohol consumption, and how should it respond to the challenges and opportunities these changes present? This was the most attempted question this year. Most candidates demonstrated a good grasp of the broad societal trends affecting alcohol consumption, and many had clearly prepared well. However, marks clustered below and around the pass mark, with relative ly few excellent performances. A handful of candidates delivered outstanding answers combining up - to - date data, well - structured analysis and genuinely original perspectives. Weaker responses tended to be descriptive, repetitive or overly focused on one area (e.g. product innovation), with limited attention to a broader strategic response or regulatory implications. No/Lo "wines" were often uncritically embraced as a panacea wi thout any real interrogation of their limitations, with some candidates devoting too much of their answer to these products. Many neglected to discuss developing markets or failed to give sufficient global examples. A further limitation in many papers was the lack of engagement with the complexity of the category's challenges and opportunities. Few candidates explored alternative strategic responses beyond product reformulation - such as changes in marketing, distribu tion, portfolio management, or consumer engagement. There was little examination of how different segments of the supply chain (from small estate producers to multinational brand owners) might experience and respond to societal shifts in consumption differ ently, or how policy interventions and health - authority messaging could shape long - term demand. Equally, realistic tensions between goals - for example, between energy - intensive alcohol removal processes and sustainability targets - were rarely mentioned. Stronger answers tackled both parts of the question clearly, defined key terms and showed a comprehensive understanding of the varied impacts across the wine supply chain. The best candidates demonstrated genuine critical thinking - particularly in interro gating the limitations of the No/Lo category (including the facts that even the most bullish current growth projections would not offset the overall decline in the wine market, and the persistent lack of real success in producing red wines in this category , which excludes a whole swathe of consumers). These candidates examined the role of global health authorities, and recognised the aforementioned tension between alcohol reduction and sustainability objectives. Better papers moved beyond health considerati ons alone, linking declining consumption among younger demographics to the evidence regarding, for example, increased cost - of - living worries and shifting social patterns, leading to changes in how leisure time is spent and a trend towards lower amounts of in - person social interaction. 3 ) You
